articles.title: Missile strikes Riyadh airport terminal, leaving multiple people wounded
articles.body:
A missile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, wounding multiple people and forcing the evacuation of passengers and suspension of flights, just two days after another deadly attack on Saudi Arabia's main international airport. The latest strike comes amid a sharp escalation in fighting between the kingdom and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels, with US President Donald Trump saying Washington is considering joining Saudi strikes against the group.
A regional official familiar with the incident told The Associated Press that the missile hit the complex housing Terminals 3 and 4, used for domestic flights, and that many people had been wounded. Ambulances rushed to the airport as passengers were evacuated. Saudi authorities subsequently confirmed that several people were injured, but did not provide a precise casualty figure.
A medical official in Riyadh told AFP that doctors had been summoned to hospitals across the capital following a "serious emergency," saying many of the casualties had suffered severe injuries. Separately, a witness told Reuters that he saw an explosion at the airport and subsequently noticed several wounded people lying on the floor inside one of its buildings.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority announced that operations at the airport had been temporarily suspended pending a damage assessment and confirmation that its facilities were safe. Media outlets affiliated with the Iranian-led regional axis claimed there were fatalities, but those reports could not immediately be verified.
The strike followed an attack on Thursday in which at least one passenger aircraft, reportedly empty at the time, was damaged and three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, were killed. Earlier attacks on airports in Riyadh and the southern city of Abha had also caused fatalities, as Houthi strikes increasingly targeted civilian aviation infrastructure.
Trump, speaking in Washington on Saturday, said the United States could become directly involved in Saudi Arabia's military campaign against the Houthis, although no decision had been made.
"We may. We're going to look at it," he told reporters. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."
Houthis seek to ‘close Saudi skies’
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, all flights bound for Riyadh were diverted or canceled following Saturday's strike. At one point, only a single helicopter was visible above the airport. Airport management urged passengers to contact their airlines before traveling to check their flight status.
Kuwait Airways announced that it had canceled flights to and from Riyadh because of the security situation. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways also canceled services, joining other carriers, including Lufthansa, that had already suspended flights to the Saudi capital earlier in the week. The US and Canadian embassies in Riyadh advised their citizens to avoid the airport.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi cities have increasingly focused on airports as part of an effort to disrupt the kingdom's aviation sector and effectively close its airspace. The rebels describe the attacks as retaliation for Saudi airstrikes against their forces in Yemen, where fighting has intensified with troops loyal to the internationally recognized Yemeni government.
Earlier this week, the Houthis warned international airlines against operating in Saudi airspace, declaring it a theater for their military operations and saying they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if carriers continued flying there. On Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree issued another message, describing it as a "final warning."
Despite the continued attacks, Saudi civil defense authorities have stopped officially reporting the activation of public warning sirens in recent days, even though alerts had been issued during previous attacks over recent months.
The latest escalation is part of a broader confrontation that resumed in July, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014. Riyadh has long supported the internationally recognized government against the Houthis, who control large parts of the country and are closely aligned with Iran.
The renewed fighting began after a Houthi attempt to break the Saudi-imposed air blockade, against the backdrop of an escalation in the war involving Iran. Last month, the rebels launched a rapid offensive and captured strategic coastal areas in southwestern Yemen overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Although the Houthis already had the ability to attack shipping with drones and missiles from a distance, their territorial gains strengthened their control over the vital maritime passage, which connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden and forms part of the shipping route between Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal. Roughly 12% of global trade passes through the route.
The importance of Bab al-Mandab, particularly for Saudi Arabia, has grown dramatically following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula during the war with Iran.
Battle for Bab al-Mandab intensifies
Earlier this week, Yemeni forces aligned with Riyadh launched a major ground offensive, dubbed "Dawn of Yemen," aimed at pushing the Houthis out of their newly captured territories and regaining control of Bab al-Mandab.
Saudi Arabia has provided extensive air support, including heavy strikes against Houthi positions. Reports indicate that pro-Saudi forces have advanced in the area, but the extent of those gains remains disputed.
Forces loyal to the Yemeni government claim they have regained control of the strategic strait, but the Houthis reject those claims. Independent accounts also differ over how much territory has been recaptured.
Houthi political bureau member Hizam al-Asad responded to the latest developments by accusing the United States and Saudi Arabia of attempting to reverse the rebels' gains.
"There is a desperate attempt by the United States and Saudi Arabia to regain control of Bab al-Mandab," he said. "We dealt a blow to the Saudi regime and to everyone who promoted the narrative that the forces loyal to the Saudi regime had taken control of Bab al-Mandab."
He also warned of further escalation.
"The operations we have carried out so far were merely a dress rehearsal. Our forces have many surprises."
Pakistan denies strikes, Turkey rules out offensive role
As the war intensifies, attention is also turning to Pakistan and Turkey, which signed a mutual defense agreement with Saudi Arabia in August, known as the Mecca Pact.
The agreement stipulates that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. It has raised questions about whether Islamabad and Ankara could be drawn into Saudi Arabia's campaign against the Houthis.
Both countries have condemned the attacks, and the alliance has agreed to activate collective defense measures. However, the extent of their potential involvement in military operations inside Yemen remains uncertain.
On Thursday, The New York Times quoted a senior Pakistani military official, speaking anonymously, as saying Pakistani fighter jets had already participated in strikes against the Houthis. Pakistan's Information Ministry denied the allegation within hours.
Pakistan has confirmed sending military personnel to Saudi Arabia. According to The New York Times, analysts monitoring the deployment estimate that approximately 8,000 Pakistani troops are stationed in the kingdom.
Another Pakistani official told the newspaper that Islamabad's assistance would focus primarily on air defenses against Houthi missiles and drones rather than offensive operations in Yemen.
Reuters also reported that Pakistan had sent military equipment to pro-Saudi forces in Aden, the southern Yemeni city where the internationally recognized government fighting the Houthis is currently based.
Turkey, meanwhile, has ruled out participating in offensive operations against the rebels.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Thursday that the Mecca Pact was "primarily a defensive alliance, not an offensive one."
According to Fidan, Turkey and Pakistan are continuing to examine how they can support Saudi Arabia against the Houthi attacks, but he stressed that Ankara would not send forces into another country to carry out an attack.
"We will not send military forces into another country's territory to conduct an offensive," he said. "We are studying how to provide Saudi Arabia with military assistance, air defense and electronic warfare capabilities under the alliance."
The distinction between defensive support and direct participation in the fighting is becoming increasingly significant as Houthi missiles continue to threaten Saudi cities, aviation infrastructure and the kingdom's economic interests. With the battle for Bab al-Mandab still unresolved and the Houthis warning that their latest strikes were only a preview, Riyadh faces the prospect of further attacks while its allies weigh how far they are prepared to go.

articles.title: Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap,' how Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
articles.body:
Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap.' How Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf- Richardson, Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.
The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining Kyiv's leverage in negotiations.
"It was not just our delegation there, but a European one as well," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "It's just that everyone was sitting there like fools."
Washington was asking Ukraine to restrain its attacks on Russian energy while giving Moscow an economic reprieve — all as Trump faced consequences from the war against Iran.
"And yet he's the one who got everyone dragged into a war in Iran — a war with no way out — and is selling us out… Just to get a temporary, deceptive reprieve a few weeks before the election," the official said.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with several Ukrainian officials involved in or close to the negotiations. All of them were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
For Ukraine, the key question was why Kyiv should surrender a major means of pressuring Moscow if Russia faced no obligation to stop attacking Ukraine's energy system.
A deal Kyiv never saw coming
President Volodymyr Zelensky had sent a Ukrainian delegation to the United States for talks scheduled for Oct. 9-10. The agenda included a possible energy ceasefire with Moscow and a separate arrangement to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Instead, the talks were derailed after Trump announced that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kyiv had not been informed of the decision in advance. Although Zelensky publicly acknowledged that Washington was considering a deal with Moscow, Ukrainian officials said they had not known the details before the announcement that evening.
For the delegation, the revelation raised questions about whether Washington had already negotiated terms with Moscow while Ukrainian and European officials were still trying to establish the parameters of an energy truce.
"It felt like a trap," the senior Ukrainian official said.
"To be honest, everyone was shocked as f*ck."
The timing of the U.S. decision only deepened the suspicion.
Following Trump's direction, the U.S. Treasury Department announced that its Office of Foreign Assets Control was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
One Ukrainian official pointed to April 7, the date on which the waiver was set to expire, as evidence that Washington had planned the measure around a specific timetable.
"They lifted the sanctions until April 7... So they were preparing this for Oct. 7. It's a birthday present for Putin. They're counting the six months," the official said.
Trump's demand to stop Ukraine's strikes
The dispute had been building for weeks.
Trump had previously pressed Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, arguing that Kyiv should stop disrupting Russia's fuel production.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told Zelensky on Sept. 13.
Kyiv rejected the premise that Ukraine should halt its strikes unilaterally. Ukrainian officials said Zelensky had repeatedly made clear that any energy ceasefire would have to apply to both sides, with Russia also stopping its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
That distinction is central to Kyiv. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, terminals, and other energy facilities aim to disrupt a major source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has systematically targeted Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
A ceasefire that stopped only Ukrainian attacks would therefore leave Russia's campaign against Ukraine's energy system intact while protecting infrastructure that helps sustain the Russian war machine.
Yet, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. negotiators presented the issue differently during the talks, framing Zelensky as responsible for the impasse because he had refused to halt attacks on Russian refineries.
The Ukrainians were also told that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing that has helped Kyiv identify and strike targets inside Russia, one person present at the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. intelligence has played an important role in Ukrainian attacks, and restricting access to it would weaken Kyiv's ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
One senior Ukrainian official involved in the talks responded with bitter humor.
"I hope the Americans don't give them Patriot (air defense systems) to protect their oil refineries," the official said.
The remark, however, captured a broader fear in Kyiv.
Washington already ended up helping Moscow shield the infrastructure that finances its war while pressuring Ukraine to surrender a means of striking back.
Another senior Ukrainian official said Ukraine had not agreed to stop attacking Russian refineries and would not commit to doing so without reciprocal Russian action.
For Kyiv, the principle remained unchanged. An energy truce could work only if both countries accepted the same restrictions.
"It was just f**king stupid to bury the idea of an energy truce with that move," one official said, suggesting that Washington was trying to strip Ukraine of its greatest source of leverage in the negotiations.
The war continues on both sides
Events on the ground showed how little the announcement had changed.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Ukrainian drones struck an oil loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don. The terminal handles petroleum products for export and supplies fuel to Russia's military.
Russia, meanwhile, launched a drone attack followed by a missile strike on Kyiv on Oct. 10, also targeting Ukrainian energy facilities.
Neither side had agreed to stop striking energy infrastructure, and the U.S. announcement had done little to bridge the gap between their positions.
Zelensky addressed the decision in a voice message to reporters late on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would just give Moscow additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
He also questioned the purpose of sending a Ukrainian delegation to negotiations under those circumstances.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," Zelensky said, calling the decision "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Ukraine was being asked to make concessions on the battlefield even as Moscow continued to attack its cities and energy infrastructure.
For one senior Ukrainian official, the explanation for Washington's move was straightforward: Trump was trying to deflect blame for the consequences of his own foreign policy.
"Clearly, Trump doesn't want to admit that it was his war against Iran that caused so many problems for Americans," the official said.

articles.title: Drones Strike Rostov Oil Terminal, Igniting Major Fire
articles.body:
Ukrainian strike drones attacked an oil transshipment terminal in the southern Russian port city of Rostov-on-Don early Saturday morning, Oct. 10, igniting a large blaze at the facility, Russian regional officials and independent media reported.
Residents across Rostov-on-Don reported multiple explosions and visible air defense fire beginning late Friday evening and continuing into the early morning hours.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rostov Regional Governor Yuriy Slyusar confirmed an aerial attack and a subsequent fire in the regional center, stating that emergency responders deployed to contain the blaze and claiming no casualties were recorded.
Slyusar said Russian air defense forces intercepted at least 50 unmanned aerial vehicles across the Rostov region between Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Open-source intelligence analysts from independent Russian news outlet Astra geolocated footage published by local residents, verifying that the fire broke out at the “Yug Rusi” oil products transshipment terminal in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district.
The facility functions as a key logistics node for petroleum products, handling transshipment from the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) and other regional suppliers.
Operating with a designed annual handling capacity of approximately 2.5 million metric tons, the terminal processes fuel supplies utilized by the Russian armed forces and facilitates maritime export shipments generating foreign currency revenue.
Putin Touts 90% Dollar-Free CIS Trade as Russia Sidesteps Western Sanctions
Although commercially known as Yug Rusi since its commissioning alongside the first phase of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in 2009, corporate filings by the Novoshakhtinsk plant designate the facility as the “NZNP oil loading terminal, Rostov branch.” The terminal was previously targeted by Ukrainian drone strikes in July.
Strategic targeting of Russian fuel and refining logistics
The strike in Rostov-on-Don forms part of a systematic Ukrainian asymmetric campaign targeting fuel depots, refineries, and chemical production hubs that sustain Moscow’s military operations.
The overnight attack follows coordinated long-range strikes on Oct. 9 that damaged Russian energy and industrial assets across western and central regions.
Drones struck the Redkino Experimental Plant in the Tver region, igniting a fire at the chemical facility, which manufactures Decylin-M – a specialized liquid fuel component utilized in Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 strategic cruise missiles – alongside fuel additives for aviation kerosene and diesel.
Concurrently on Oct. 9, Ukrainian strikes hit an oil depot north of Belgorod that supplies fuel to industrial enterprises and transport fleets across the border region, while a separate drone strike damaged a major Yandex data center in Kaluga, disabling multiple server modules for the second consecutive day following an earlier strike on a company facility in Sasovo, Ryazan region.
Extended-range interdiction
Ukrainian precision units have progressively expanded their operational strike radius against Russian petrochemical infrastructure deep inside Russia.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) announced they conducted a second deep-interdiction strike against the Omsk Oil Refinery in southwestern Siberia, situated roughly 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Operating alongside the domestic Russian insurgent movement “Chernaya Iskra” (Black Spark), SSO long-range strike drones navigated flight routes approaching 3,000 kilometers to strike distillation units at the Siberian plant.
Ukrainian defense and security officials have emphasized that degrading refining capacity, export terminals, and frontline fuel stockpiles directly constrains the mobility of Russian mechanized units while diminishing state export earnings that fund the Kremlin’s wartime budget.

articles.title: Ukraine attacks Russia with spy balloons
articles.body:
Ukraine attacks Russia with spy balloons
Ukrainian spy balloons have been spotted over central Russia’s Yaroslavl Region for the first time, according to the regional Security Ministry.
Local authorities said several of the small flying objects were successfully shot down on Friday, urging residents to report anything suspicious that they see in the sky or suspected debris to emergency services.
The balloons “had been launched from the territory of Ukraine,” according to officials. Small reconnaissance balloons can be used to distract enemy air defenses, but they can also serve as reconnaissance platforms, including to pinpoint the locations of air defense systems or help direct strikes against other targets.
Yaroslavl Region has been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes in recent weeks. In mid-September, the Russian military shot down 65 drones over the region in a single day during a large-scale drone raid targeting a local refinery.
Although Friday’s incident was the first of its kind reported in Yaroslavl Region, the Russian military has encountered Ukrainian spy balloons and even explosive-laden balloons in the past.
In September 2025, the Ukrainian military attempted to strike several Russian regions with dozens of meteorological balloons carrying explosives.
The Wall Street Journal claimed in a February article that Kiev had been using high-altitude balloons in attacks on Russia since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. However, according to the Russian Defense Ministry, such attacks were first detected in autumn 2024, with another surge in reported incidents in late summer 2025.
The recent balloon attacks come as Russia has stepped up strikes on missile and drone warehouses, as well as unmanned aerial vehicle assembly facilities, in response to continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure, which Moscow describes as terrorist acts.
After Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky recently threatened to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries, Moscow vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military-related facilities while maintaining that it never targets civilians.
On Wednesday, the Russian military targeted a Smart Ammunition facility used to assemble and store FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, FP-9 tactical ballistic missiles, and components for both weapons, as well as other sites across several Ukrainian regions, including a drone workshop in Kirovograd Region and the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in Kremenchug, which Russian officials say is used to manufacture small-arms ammunition.

articles.title: Finland to send F-16 ammunition to Ukraine within days
articles.body:
Finland will supply ammunition for Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets within the coming days, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced on Saturday, 10 October, following a telephone conversation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The delivery forms part of Finland's 35th military assistance package to Ukraine, valued at approximately €1 million, as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks across the country.
Zelenskyy disclosed the planned shipment in a Facebook post following his discussion with Stubb. He said the ammunition would help Ukrainian forces intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones, which Moscow has deployed in attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
The Ukrainian president did not specify the type or quantity of ammunition Finland would provide.
Stubb also confirmed the conversation in a post on X, stating that air defence was a central component of Finland's latest military assistance package.
The Finnish Ministry of Defence announced the package on Friday, 9 October, after the government accelerated its response to an urgent request from Kyiv.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said Helsinki had brought forward its decision because of Ukraine's immediate defence requirements.
"We will not close our eyes to Ukrainians’ hour of need. Instead, we will stand with Ukraine and continue our materiel assistance deliveries," Häkkänen said in the ministry's statement.
The Finnish president formally approved the shipment on 9 October following a government proposal.
According to the Defence Ministry, the package consists of a single category of military equipment drawn from Finnish Defence Forces stocks.
The announcement brings the total value of Finland's military equipment assistance to Ukraine to approximately €3.6 billion since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Helsinki has also begun preparing another, more extensive assistance package, although officials have not announced its value or expected delivery date.
Ukraine has relied on Western-supplied F-16 aircraft to strengthen its air defences and counter Russian aerial attacks.
Denmark and the Netherlands supplied approximately 40 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine during 2024 and 2025. Ukrainian authorities have not disclosed how many remain operational.
During Saturday's conversation, Zelenskyy and Stubb also discussed the recent agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin concerning Russian diesel supplies to American and international markets.
Russian strikes across south-eastern Ukraine early on Saturday killed 15 people, including three children. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of responding to the US decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports by launching five glide bombs at residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
Zelenskyy described the agreement as a new challenge and said Ukraine and Finland were coordinating further diplomatic discussions and responses.
Earlier in the week, Russian attacks reportedly killed nearly 80 civilians across Ukraine over two days.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1689: Russia plans up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs against 60 Ukrainian infrastructure sites this winter, Ukraine says
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare. Ukrainian forces combined assaults with drones and ground robots to reclaim territory in Donetsk Oblast while limiting their exposure to Russian fire.
More than 500 drones by Moscow’s count: Kh-101 fuel plant, second Yandex data center, and a far-north refinery hit. Russian officials confirmed the fires but named none of the targets.
Ukraine reruns its Vivaldi playbook outside Kramatorsk and pushes Russia back across the Siverskyi Donets, ISW says. Even Russian milbloggers now concede Ukrainian gains east of Sloviansk, including a river crossing toward a key height.
Drone attack forces Yandex to shut down its data center on the grounds of a sanctioned Russian machine-tool plant. In Bashkortostan, Ukraine’s General Staff says its forces hit a Gazprom refinery. Salavat’s mayor says an unnamed enterprise there keeps working.
Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says. The faster drones break through Ukraine’s air defenses more reliably, and ISW expects the same strike pattern in Russia’s winter campaign against Ukraine’s energy.
Intelligence and technology
Air-raid sirens cost Kyiv’s weapons makers 61.8 working hours in month, nearly eight days, yet their contract deadlines stay fixed, two groups say. Ukraine’s gunmakers want the government to count real siren downtime against contract deadlines.
Ukrainian producer that neutralized more than 7,000 drones over 100 square kilometers in year, plays enemy in Pentagon contest, and gets invitation to continue. Ukraine’s Phantom Defense built the counter-drone environment for the Pentagon’s Gauntlet II.
Ukraine uses up Europe’s yearly supply of thermal sensors in about five months, so two Ukrainian firms will build their own plants in the West. Their new venture wants to give Western armies their own supply of the chip that lets thermal cameras see body heat in the dark.
Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites. Substations near Ukraine’s western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe, could be among the first targets.
International
Trump says Russia agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel to US and global markets as he blames Ukraine for fuel price hikes driven by Iran war. The announcement comes as Trump pressures Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil infrastructure, which Ukraine targets to weaken Moscow’s war economy.
Head of Russian military propaganda network to be expelled from Montenegro over suspected anti-EU operation. Authorities ordered Mikhail Zvynchuk, founder of the Russian military-focused Rybar network, and four associates to leave the country after seizing drones and recording equipment.
Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated. Tkach says armed people smashed the car windows, forced the journalists onto the road, and put a knee on his neck during the detention.
Russia sells cheaper fuel abroad and pays to keep its own pumps running amid Ukraine’s refinery strikes, but crude money still flows. After Ukraine’s drone strikes on refineries, Russia’s diesel exports, once its biggest fuel export, fell to a decade low.
Fought against Ukraine, now claimed to be victims: Kenya’s plea for five men held by Ukraine. Kenya says the men took Russian army contracts under false job promises.
Moldova pulls its border officers off Ukrainian soil again as Russian drones keep hitting crossings. “They will work on the territory of Moldova.” Moldovan Interior Minister Daniela Misail-Nikitin, on withdrawing border personnel from Ukraine.
Lithuania puts up to 100 soldiers on Kaliningrad border as officials brace for possible Russian mobilization. The move comes as Moscow rejects reports of a new call-up while Ukrainian officials warn Russia is preparing to expand its forces.
80% of Moldovans say country is unprepared for attack as Russian drones flow into its airspace, but few back NATO membership. A new poll shows widespread concern over Moldova’s ability to withstand an attack, even as only 4% of respondents see NATO membership as the answer. Russian drones have increasingly crossed Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
Polish SIM cards found inside Russian drones in Poland, raising new questions over 2025 incursion. More than 30 Russian drones entered Polish airspace in September 2025, and some were found carrying Polish SIM cards, RMF24 reports.
Ukraine’s FM links Russian plague scare to history of cover-ups, from anthrax to Chornobyl and COVID-19. Russia’s handling of the suspected case fits a broader pattern of concealing information about dangerous incidents, Andrii Sybiha said.
Humanitarian and social impact
Eggs cost nearly 20 times US prices in occupied Oleshky, where Ukraine’s ombudsman says people die of hunger every day. Residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky cannot leave the city and are waiting for an opportunity to evacuate through a humanitarian corridor.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy. Three people were killed and a woman was still missing as the outages spread.
Blackouts return to Kyiv as Russia prepares to freeze civilians over the winter. Russia is once again targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as winter approaches, threatening to leave civilians without power, heat, and water as Moscow ramps up its campaign to cripple the country’s critical systems.
Two 14-year-old boys killed by an explosive device in a field in Sumy Oblast. Residents are being warned that, in addition to constant Russian attacks, there is a risk of encountering explosive devices.
Russia kills 30 in strike on two passenger buses in Kramatorsk. Hours after the strike, the head of Donetsk Oblast ordered public transport in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk halted, saying Russia had made the buses a target.
A 3-year-old girl came to visit her aunt in Pryluky, Ukraine. By morning, a Russian missile had killed her grandmother and uncle. Zlatoslava is in hospital in Chernihiv. Her aunt, a police officer, was wounded in the strike.
Political and legal developments
Investigators say prosecutors shielded scam call centers. Their office has now fired eight people and is checking how its ex-chief left Ukraine. The acting chief also ordered out a deputy at the regional office he ran until September and dropped no-contest hiring of outsiders.

articles.title: Finland to Supply F-16 Ammunition to Counter Jet Drones, Zelensky Says
articles.body:
Ukraine will receive specialized ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets from Finland in the coming days to intercept Russian turbojet-powered strike drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Saturday, Oct. 10.
Speaking following a telephone consultation with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Zelensky expressed gratitude for Helsinki’s swift defense assistance, emphasizing that the incoming munitions are essential for neutralizing high-speed loitering munitions that challenge ground-based defenses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“I spoke with President of Finland Alexander Stubb. I am particularly grateful for the support package for our sky defense,” Zelensky stated on social media. “In the coming days, we will receive ammunition for F-16s. This is what currently ensures the downing of jet-powered Shaheds.”
The president reported that the bilateral discussion covered recent Russian aerial strikes against Ukrainian cities and municipal infrastructure, as well as joint diplomatic countermeasures to restrict Russian revenues derived from petroleum product exports.
“Naturally, we also discussed a new challenge: additional Russian revenues from the export of petroleum products, which could go toward financing further Russian aggression,” Zelensky said. “We are preparing meetings and coordinating steps that could be useful in the current circumstances.”
Belarus Summons Ukraine Envoy Over Alleged Bryansk Drone Strike
The munitions transfer follows Helsinki’s approval on Friday of its 35th defense materiel assistance package for Kyiv. Valued at approximately €1 million ($1.13 million), the emergency package was expedited following an urgent appeal by Ukrainian defense authorities and drew a single, undisclosed defense asset directly from Finnish military stockpiles.
Rising threat of high-speed turbojet loitering munitions
The provision of aircraft munitions arrives as Ukrainian military commanders warn that Moscow is rapidly transitioning its long-range drone arsenal toward turbine-propelled models that outpace conventional low-altitude interception networks.
Russian forces have accelerated the deployment of jet-powered Shahed variants since July, presenting significant tactical hurdles for mobile air defense fire teams reliant on heavy machine guns and propeller-driven counter-drone aircraft. While baseline piston-engine Shahed-136 drones cruise at speeds between 180 and 200 km/h, current Russian turbojet drones fly at roughly 600 km/h (370 mph).
Ukrainian Air Force commanders anticipate that adversary technology will continue to advance. During an address to a parliamentary investigative commission, Deputy Air Force Commander Colonel Yurii Cherevashenko warned that Russian designers could eventually increase the dash velocity of jet-powered strike drones to between 800 and 900 km/h (500 to 560 mph).
“We have not seen such speeds yet, but we forecast them,” Cherevashenko said.
Cherevashenko noted that jet-powered drones currently constitute roughly 40 percent of unmanned strike waves deployed against Ukraine, with their share reaching up to 60 percent along specific operational axes.
Military planners project that high-speed turbine models could eventually comprise up to 80 percent of all Russian strike drone salvos, drastically compressing warning times and forcing Ukrainian defenders to rely more heavily on combat aviation.

articles.title: Why won’t the world call Russia’s theft of Ukrainian children genocide? A Ukrainian lawyer has the evidence, and says only the will is missing.
articles.body:
Kateryna Rashevska can trace exactly how one Ukrainian child disappears into Russia: the occupied-territory orphanage, the foster placement with a Kremlin-connected family, the re-education camp, the military uniform, the draft notice that arrives at sixteen. A legal expert at Ukraine's Regional Center for Human Rights, she has filed submissions to the International Criminal Court, documented the cases behind recent EU sanctions, and spent years building the argument that this is not only a war crime but genocide.
The law, she says, is ready. In less than five years of war, Russia has forcibly transferred at least 20,651 Ukrainian children from occupied Ukraine, a crime that has already put President Vladimir Putin and his children's-rights commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in the dock of the ICC. The 1948 Genocide Convention lists the forcible transfer of children as one of the acts that constitute genocide, and the ICC's Ukraine investigation has been mandated to examine the charge since 2022. More than 150 states have signed that convention. None has been willing to say the word about Russia.
"We don't need to change any legal framework," Rashevska says. "We simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names." She presses the point because, for her, justice is not an afterthought but a deterrent: "Without justice, Russia will feel this resentment in several years, and they will repeat their actions."
And the court that could deliver that justice is collapsing. The ICC is in the deepest crisis of its existence: its prosecutor, Karim Khan, removed, 13 of its judges and prosecutors sanctioned by the United States, and on 9 October 2026 the court itself sanctioned by Washington for the first time, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick." The court called the move unprecedented and warned that "history will judge this moment."
Meanwhile the children remain. Of the more than 20,000 taken, only 2,665 have been returned, as of 7 October 2026. The rest are placed in Russia's adoption system and foster homes, taught to forget they are Ukrainian, to love Russia, and to be willing to die for it: Rashevska cites 344,000 Ukrainian children drawn into the Movement of the First and 55,000 into the Yunarmiya youth army.
Euromaidan Press spoke with Rashevska on the sidelines of GLOBSEC 2026 in Prague about the machine Russia built to steal a generation, and why the world still won't name it.
Alya: You say that Russia’s forcible transfer of Ukrainian children is the crime of genocide. In international law, genocide is defined by Article 6 of the Rome Statute. What would it take to change this legal framework to include the deportation and militarization of Ukrainian children? And is the Office of the Prosecutor in any position to do that work under current US sanctions and Karim Khan’s leave?
Kateryna: We don’t need to change any legal frameworks to prosecute what the Russians are doing with Ukrainian children. Militarization and political indoctrination, as well as Russification of young Ukrainians, is a part of Russia’s bigger strategy to destroy Ukraine as a sovereign state and to subjugate everything in the Ukrainian nation to the Russian influence and control. I don’t see legal problems; we simply still lack the political will to call the crimes by their proper names.
The UN’s 1948 Genocide Convention posits that all states that signed the convention, 154 as of today, should act to stop it—not only those affected by genocide. If the international community recognized what the Russians are doing as a crime of genocide, it would mean that yet another time in history the international community was not able to prevent genocide, to recognize some early warnings, to react properly to what the Russians did, for example, in occupied Crimea or Donbas before 2022. It is not easy, and the international community and world political leaders should be mature enough to face all these challenges, recognize that they were involved in the commission of these crimes through silence and inaction, and finally stop it.
So that is why, according to the Rome Statute, the Office of the Prosecutor can start an investigation of the crime of genocide in the Ukrainian context. It is possible: the ICC’s Ukraine-situation investigation in March 2022, supported by 43 states, included not only war crimes and crimes against humanity, but also the crime of genocide. So we have all the legal tools and means, but politically it is very difficult.
Recently, there has been a global shift towards this—in the context of the war between Arabian states and Israel, not Ukraine. But for example, Israel’s attacks against Gaza’s education have already been termed "scholasticide," so as a part of the genocidal intent, as a part of the crime of genocide. So for us lawyers and human rights defenders, this is the task—to push the international community to do the same with Russia. It is not easy because Russia is one of the five "world policemen" expected to maintain this international legal order.
I believe that, perhaps in decades, but we will see how Russia’s actions will be recognized as the crime of genocide. The forcible transfer of children from one group to another group is the fifth universally recognized element of the crime of genocide.
Alya: Your organization was involved in documenting this. How does this pipeline actually work?
Kateryna: Yes, let's take Olga Druzhinina, who fostered four children from the occupied territories of Ukraine. Her story is very interesting: first, it seemed that she could be just an ordinary Russian brainwashed by TV shows about children from Donbas. But then we found that Olga is very close to [former Russian President] Medvedev, and through Medvedev to President Putin. Olga is the head of one non-governmental organization, "Semia Arktiki" [Family of the Arctic], and this organization aims to find foster parents for orphans— now including orphans from occupied territories of Ukraine. The co-head of this organization also fostered Ukrainian children.
It is a very well-built, pre-planned architecture of people involved in the commission of this crime—not some sporadic reaction to the full-scale invasion. They planned to do it. And I will not be surprised if, in the future, we find that these families also adopted children from Crimea or from Donbas even before 2022.
Her husband is a veteran of the Russian Armed Forces. He participated in many wars of the Russian regime, including the wars in Chechnya. It was clearly against the child's best interest to be sent to the family of this Russian serviceman and his wife. So their case was widely publicized. We recorded many different details. Later, we found photos of these children in the "Warrior Center" camp in Novosibirsk, and her foster daughter from occupied Ukraine wearing a St.George’s [Russian imperial] ribbon and in military uniform.
So the Ukrainian identity of these children was completely eradicated. It was prohibited to mention that they were Ukrainians, and the main goal of this family was to repress their unloyalty to the Russian state, to re-educate them, mold them into Russian patriots. Unfortunately, I don’t know the fate of these teenagers from Mariupol, but as far as I know, they were not returned to Ukraine. And now they are already young adults—meaning they will soon be conscripted into the Russian army. They have this military duty because they were forcibly given Russian citizenship. And young children also remain under the control of Olga and his husband.
Olga and her husband are members of the so-called "Putin Team." They were recognized many times as the best family of the Yamalo-Nenets region. The governor of Yamal-Nenets is also Putin's person. His candidacy was supported by Putin for re-election to this position. And this governor has many times mentioned that Ukrainian children from the occupied territories of Ukraine were accepted by foster families from his region, even without the proper documents.
It is very difficult to influence their behavior without sanctions. In this sphere of foster care, the balance between placing children in Russian institutions and Russian families is hard to find. Russia presents only two options for the forcibly transferred Ukrainian children: Russian boarding institutions or Russian foster families. And of course, ordinary people think: a family is better than a boarding institution. The truth is that there is a third option: just return these children to Ukraine, to their homes.
And I would like to highlight that, according to the order of Ukrainian President Zelenskyy, these children from institutions will not be returned to boarding institutions in Ukraine. They will inevitably be placed with a foster family, and they can participate in choosing this family or changing it. Ukraine is doing its best to guarantee that its actions comply with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, but unfortunately, Russians are very hard to persuade to return these orphanage children.
Alya: On 11 May 2026, the EU Council sanctioned 16 individuals and seven entities for the systematic unlawful deportation, forced transfer, and forced assimilation of Ukrainian children, including through indoctrination and militarized education. Your organization pushed for these sanctions. Are they working?
Kateryna: In January–February 2026, we criticized the European Union’s sanctions policy. New persons were being added to lists, but we found that the level of coordination and harmonization of sanctions policies was only 5%. Only 13 individuals and three organizations were under sanctions in all jurisdictions analyzed by us: Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Canada, the United States, the European Union, Switzerland, and Japan. It was terrifying because sanctions exist, yet they are riddled by many loopholes and are actually inefficient.
Trending Now
That is why we started persuading them to do something with this system. And on 11 May, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the European Union synchronized their sanctions packages: the people are included in all jurisdictions. For us, this is a big achievement.
Another achievement: a shift in their perception of where this vertical of guilty persons ends. Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova—okay; ministers, children's rights ombudspersons at the regional level, heads of the occupation authorities—okay. But what about the "ordinary" Russian people who fostered poor Ukrainian children and now contribute to their militarization? The 11 May sanctions saw the United Kingdom and Canada listing ordinary Russians, like the family from Yamalo-Nenets that fostered four Ukrainian children, including teenagers from Mariupol, and then sent them to re-education camps of the "Center Warrior" to be militarized as Russian soldiers.
If these results of our work seem small, we must remember that for the Russians, it is a very sensitive issue. They are mad because of the sanctions—and this was visible when the “Yolochka” boarding institution in occupied Crimea’s Simferopol, called a “concentration camp” by ordinary Russians, was sanctioned. Already in December 2014 [after Russia’s occupation of east Ukraine], the first Ukrainian orphans were sent to Russian foster families from this “Yolochka.” 12 years later, children from Kherson boarding institutions also went through “Yolochka.”
Alya: You've documented over 20,500 deported children. How many of that cohort are approaching Russian conscription age?
Kateryna: It is hard to tell because the way the Ukrainian side is collecting statistics is not good enough. So you should address this question to the competent bodies of Ukraine.
But according to our calculations, just to describe the situation in general: all Ukrainian teenagers under Russian control start receiving draft notices at the age of 16. According to the Russian legislation, it should be at the age of 17, but they're so afraid that these children will escape or will return to Ukrainian-controlled territories, that they start this process in violation of their own legislation.
Everything is organized around schools. They’re not about education under occupation, but have become additional buildings of the military commissariat. Specific teachers are responsible for this conscription process. Boys aged 16-17 are being brought to the military commissariat in organized groups. You cannot escape, you cannot refuse, because you will hear “knock-knock” on your door: the occupation authorities and your teacher will ask: “Where are you? You should go.”
Another problem: Russia and Belarus started exchanging data, meaning that if this child receives a draft notice at the age of 18, he will not be able to cross the border—which matters because the checkpoint of Mokrany-Domanove between Belarus and Ukraine is the main point of returning Ukrainian children from Russian control. Every year, the Russians amend their legislation to impose more obstacles to the repatriation process.
So the only way for a Ukrainian teenage boy to escape is to do this several days before a "povestka" [draft notice] comes to his house at 16 years.
According to our intelligence, since 2014, 48,000 Ukrainians from occupied territories were forcibly mobilized by Russians, including those from occupied Crimea. Some of them participated in the "special military operation.” Around 20% of all prisoners of war in Ukrainian camps for Russians are originally Ukrainians who were forced to sign a military contract. Many of them were forced, manipulated, or brainwashed, so it was not done of their own will.
But I would like to highlight that the average age of a Russian soldier is 35. This is not the war of young Ukrainians who reached the age of majority and were sent to the battlefield as cannon fodder. We see that the Russians’ main goal is to rebuild the army degraded by the Ukrainian side during the first month of the full-scale invasion, to have officers and other qualified personnel who will develop a strategy and conquer more and more territory. That is why they're investing in all these military patriotic movements and centers.
That is why I was really impressed when I saw that their All-Russian championship on drone racing will be for children aged seven. Should we next expect that children in kindergartens will assemble and disassemble a rifle? Their society is very militarized. This is the biggest problem. And now, Russian soldiers are those who are teaching Ukrainian children to fight tomorrow.
Alya: Thank you so much, Kateryna, for your time.

articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
articles.body:
Donald Trump is on a fresh collision course with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Vladimir Putin on Friday, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
The Ukrainian president said “back room deals” with the Russian leader would give Putin more chances on the battlefield. On Saturday morning, Ukrainian officials reported that a Russian attack had killed 12 people in the south-east, including three children, and Moscow claimed its troops were advancing in the east.
In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war against Iran.
“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia,” he said, to deliver millions of tonnes of diesel fuel over the next few months.
He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”
Fuel prices have soared since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – a gallon of regular fuel in the US is about $4.20 (£3.17) – it is the price of diesel, which last month hit a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most damage on Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm elections approach.
Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need it to operate machinery.
Democrats said the agreement undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.
“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” said a statement from the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the banking committee.
Some Republicans also criticised the agreement.
“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”
Zelenskyy told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 this week.
In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.
“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Referring on Saturday to the attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 12 people, Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.
“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”
Separately, Russian media cited the defence ministry as saying its forces had captured the settlements of Lukashove and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelenskyy previously said Putin had been playing games with Trump, and on Saturday, a Kremlin spokesperson said the Russian leader had responded with “understanding” to Trump’s proposals to de-escalate the conflict.
Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.
Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.
“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.
Trump recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Tensions have been rising between Russia and European Nato members amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.
The latest development is likely to worsen Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”
But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment at his failure to reach a peace deal.
Trump’s willingness to reach a fuel agreement with Putin comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of US forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

articles.title: US Envoys Pressure Kyiv on Refinery Strikes
articles.body:
US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have warned Ukrainian negotiators during high-level talks in Miami that Washington could cut off intelligence sharing if Kyiv does not halt long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Accodring to Axios, the reported ultimatum came amid escalating friction over a bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and international markets – a transaction the White House claimed would alleviate elevated consumer fuel prices.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A US official disputed that the American envoys issued an explicit threat, but confirmed that Witkoff and Kushner conveyed that Washington expected reciprocity from Kyiv given US deliveries of ammunition and intelligence, warning that Ukrainian actions should not harm American consumers.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told Axios. “[President Volodymyr] Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the goodwill that he has built with Trump over the last six months.”
According to Axios, the talks in Miami centered on finalizing post-war security guarantees that the US, Europe, and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a settlement framework to end the conflict, alongside prospective territorial compromise proposals.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Witkoff and Kushner presented a post-war reconstruction and security package, with discussions addressing Ukraine’s accession path to the EU, post-war relations with NATO, and a durable European security architecture.
Trump’s diesel pivot
The diplomatic rift deepened after Zelensky rejected US demands for a unilateral halt to deep strikes on Russian petrochemical assets.
Ukrainian officials had proposed a mutual energy armistice, conveying to Trump, Witkoff, and Kushner that Kyiv would suspend strikes on Russian oil refineries if Moscow concurrently halted missile and drone bombardments against Ukraine’s electricity grid and heating plants.
However, Trump insisted on an unconditional, unilateral suspension of strikes on Russian refining facilities, arguing that the operations contributed directly to domestic fuel inflation ahead of winter.
The US president did not view strikes on Russian commercial refineries as equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure, the US official told Axios.
“President Trump decided to strike the diesel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen US requests to stop attacking Russian refineries,” the official stated.
In an interview with Axios following the White House announcement, Zelensky described the agreement as an unexpected and “unfair” development, characterizing the sanctions waiver as an unjustified concession to Putin.
The US official maintained that the administration seeks to engage Moscow in diplomatic negotiations, asserting that while Putin continues to strike Ukrainian territory, Washington assesses the Kremlin remains open to discussions on concluding the war if an acceptable framework is presented.
Refining deficits and operational defiance
The friction over refinery targeting unfolds as Ukrainian officials reaffirm that Kyiv will not abandon asymmetric deep strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Financial Times on Saturday that Ukraine intends to press ahead with drone strikes on refineries, stating plainly: “We will burn [Russian] refineries.”
Energy market analysts have expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s physical capacity to fulfill the export volumes announced by Trump, citing extensive operational damage across the Russian refining sector.
Independent market tracking by intelligence firm Kpler indicates that Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of installed capacity due to emergency maintenance and equipment deficits caused by Ukrainian drone waves.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel monthly by sea, but maritime shipments collapsed throughout 2026 as successive strikes idled primary distillation and cracking units across European Russia and Siberia. Constrained refining output prompted the Kremlin to enact an export ban on domestic diesel in July to stave off domestic fuel deficits.
Trump’s announcement claimed Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Following the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
The waiver was enacted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which aimed to expand statutory sanctions across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.

articles.body:
Live: Trump lashes out at Zelensky, says Ukraine needs new president who will agree to end war
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said that Ukraine needs a new president “who can make a deal” to end the war. He also called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to stop hitting Russian oil refineries. This comes after Washington moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel and Moscow's continued strikes on Ukraine killed at least 21 people, including four children. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
Ukraine's FM says Zelensky 'deserves support', after Trump calls for new president
Ukraine's foreign minister said President Volodymyr Zelensky had the backing of the Ukrainian people and deserved support after US President Donald Trump called for him to be replaced.
"He has the support of the Ukrainian people, and they have the right to decide," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said of Zelensky in a post on X.
"Statements from abroad only confirm that he is doing his job well. He deserves support."
Russian negotiator welcomes Trump call for new Ukraine president
Russian President Vladimir Putin's top economic negotiator on Saturday welcomed Donald Trump's call for a new Ukrainian president, describing the US leader's remarks as "iconic and historic".
"President Trump joins the many who believe that Ukraine needs leadership actually focused on peace, not Zelensky's warmongering ... Iconic and historic," Kirill Dmitriev, the Kremlin's special envoy on economic cooperation, said in a post on X.
Trump says Zelensky 'better damn well stop' hitting Russian refineries, urges new leader
US President Donald Trump called for new leadership in Ukraine, slamming Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and calling on Kyiv's leader to stop hitting Russian oil refineries.
"He better damn well stop," Trump told reporters at the White House, one day after saying he had struck a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel to global markets.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," he said, referring to Zelensky.
🎥 Family mourns young girl killed in strike
Early Saturday, Russia targeted residential neighbourhoods in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia with "five guided aerial bombs", according to Ukraine's National Police. At least 15 people were killed, including three children, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
The family of a young girl killed in the attack was inconsolable.
Russia says its drones hit Kyiv data-processing centre and cargo ship
Russia’s Defence Ministry said its drones had struck a data-processing centre in Kyiv earlier on Saturday and a cargo ship carrying military supplies to the Ukrainian port of Odesa.
In a statement, the ministry said the Kyiv facility was used by Ukraine’s armed forces to collect, process and store intelligence.
Reuters could not immediately verify the reports.
🎥 Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15
Fifteen people, including three children, were killed in a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Saturday, a day after US President Donald Trump announced a deal to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, in a major setback for Kyiv.
Our correspondent Gulliver Cragg tells us more.
Ukrainian delegation heads home after Miami talks
A delegation of Ukrainian officials who visited Miami for talks on ending Russia's war in Ukraine was heading home on Saturday, an aide to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
"The groups are already on their way home," Dmytro Lytvyn, an advisor to the president, told reporters in response to an AFP question.
US envoys Witkoff and Kushner may visit Moscow in next two weeks, TASS cites source
US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have spearheaded efforts to broker a Ukraine peace agreement, may visit Moscow within the next two weeks, Russian state news agency TASS reported, citing a source.
EU top diplomat says lifting diesel sanctions gives Russia 'revenues to wage war'
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said lifting sanctions on Russian diesel helped fuel the Kremlin's war on Ukraine, after US President Donald Trump announced a deal for Moscow to supply fuel.
"Russian strikes killed over 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days. Moreover, it has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO allies," Kallas posted online.
"Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't," she wrote.
Macron expresses 'solidarity' with Zelensky 'in the face of ongoing attacks'
French President Emmanuel Macron spoke on Saturday with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky to “express solidarity” on behalf of France “in the face of the ongoing attacks” by Russia, as 15 people were killed in Russian bombings on Zaporizhzhia.
“The President of the Republic spoke today with President Zelensky to express our solidarity in the face of the ongoing attacks,” the head of state’s office said.
The Élysée did not immediately react to US President Donald Trump’s announcement of a deal on the delivery of Russian diesel to the US and global markets, accompanied by a lifting of sanctions on Moscow.

'Large-scale power outages' in Kyiv following Russian strikes
Ukraine's capital Kyiv suffered "large-scale power outages" on Saturday because of Russian strikes, the country's largest private energy provider said.
"New large-scale power outages in the capital due to attacks. Stabilisation schedules are currently not in effect," DTEK, a private energy firm, said in a statement on Telegram.
🎥 Trump hails Russia deal to release diesel as midterms loom
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had secured Russia's agreement for a major release of diesel, as he eased sanctions on Moscow to lower energy costs ahead of midterm elections.
Four civilians killed in Russian-held Luhansk region over past 24 hours, Moscow-installed governor says
Four civilians were killed and five others were wounded as a result of Ukrainian attacks on the Russian-controlled Luhansk region in eastern Ukraine in the past 24 hours, the region's Russian-installed governor Leonid Pasechnik said.
Reuters could not independently verify the report and there was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

Germany to pursue new sanctions on Russia despite US diesel deal
Germany said it would continue to push for new EU sanctions against Russia despite Moscow's agreement with Washington to release diesel to ease a fuel crunch.
"The German government sticks to its measures sanctioning Russia and is working jointly with its European partners on new sanctions," government spokesman Stefan Kornelius said in a statement sent to AFP.
Major backer Germany's "support for Ukraine in its struggle to defend itself remains unfailing", he added.
"Diplomatic efforts for a peaceful solution continue."
Moscow has been hit with waves of sanctions by the United States and partners since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
