articles.body:
The US embassy in Riyadh said it was aware of attacks on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital on Saturday and advised its citizens to avoid the airport and surrounding areas.
Breadcrumb
The New Arab's live blog has now closed. Below are some of the top stories from today:
Kuwait Airways said on Saturday it had cancelled flights to and from the Saudi capital Riyadh due to what it described as the closure of Riyadh airport because of the "security situation".
The Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia on Saturday warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh's international airport after reports it was attacked.
Spain's embassy, in a message on X, alerted nationals to a "new attack" on the airport, where witnesses earlier told AFP an evacuation was ordered.
A diplomatic source separately told AFP that Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis had hit the airport with a missile.
A diplomatic source told AFP that Yemen's Houthis hit the Riyadh airport on Saturday with a missile at around 3:00 pm local time.
"Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target," said the source, who had been briefed on the matter.
London is currently witnessing large-scale pro-Palestine protests, with organisers from the Palestine Solidarity Coalition saying 250,000 people took part in the demo.
Demonstrators made their way to Westminster, with several keynote speakers giving speeches to crowds, including MP for Hayes and Harlington, John McDonnell, who said that "we want to see Israel economically and politically isolated", including the expulsion of Israel's ambassador to the UK.
Zara Sultana MP, during her speech, said: "We need to be clear: this is not some distant tragedy beyond our control, the British government has choices to make, and Andy Burnham must be held to account because you cannot claim to stand for human rights while continuing to sell arms to a genocidal state."
Jeremy Corbyn MP told crowds that "It's time for the British government to acknowledge that a genocide is taking place."
According to the Metropolitan Police, several arrests have been made, including against a man and a woman who held placards in support of the proscribed group Palestine Action.
People were being evacuated from Riyadh's international airport on Saturday, witnesses told AFP, raising fears of a fresh attack after strikes claimed by Yemen's Houthis killed three people there this week.
Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and at least one person was injured in an unspecified incident at the airport, a relative told AFP.
The relative said the person suffered injuries to their shoulders and arms from shattered glass and was being taken to hospital.
Two other witnesses confirmed people were being evacuated, but did not know what triggered it.
The airport was hit by deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Houthis on Thursday, though the Iran-backed group did not announce any fresh strikes on the facility on Saturday.
People at Riyadh's international airport were being evacuated from the facility on Saturday, three witnesses told AFP, as officials called on passengers to check their flight status before heading there.
One witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, while the other two witnesses were not able to confirm what incident triggered the evacuation.
A loud blast was heard at the airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on Saturday, an eyewitness and people briefed on the matter told Reuters.
The Saudi government media office and the Saudi civil aviation authority did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree on Saturday cancelling legislative elections scheduled for 28 November 2026 and setting presidential and legislative elections for 11 September 2027, the official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.
Yemeni military sources told AFP on Saturday their forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait but have not yet secured control of the waterway, after the government launched an operation to recapture lost territory.
The Saudi-backed government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the pro-Iran group seized Yemen's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandeb area but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
Sources from the military of Yemen's internationally recognised government also said Mayun Island in the heart of the strait remained in Houthi hands as fighting continued.
Clashes in western Yemen, specifically around the strait, had killed at least 63 people in the past 24 hours, military sources from both sides told AFP on Saturday.
After 12 years on the ground, the last troops from the International Coalition that fought the Islamic State (IS) departed Iraq last week.
It was a comparatively quiet occasion compared with the composed exit by the US in 2011 or the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. It nevertheless marks a new chapter for Iraq, which from now on will have less international support and fewer eyes upon it.
A major question is whether Iraq will be able to manage its own security without the stabilising presence of US and Coalition troops. The last time it was in this position, Baghdad failed spectacularly, and foreign troops were back within three years.
An eight-year-old Palestinian girl has been killed after being fired on by an Israeli quadcopter drone in the al-Jawazat area of Gaza City, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.
The agency also said a Palestinian woman was injured by Israeli fire in Khan Younis.
The Kremlin said on Saturday that President Vladimir Putin relayed to US President Donald Trump Iran's position on a possible resolution to the US-Iran war, with the backing of the Iranian president, Russia's Interfax news agency reported.
"In coordination with the president of Iran, Putin conveyed to Trump the Iranian side's view on a possible resolution of the conflict," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted as saying.
The leader of Iran's Crisis Management Organisation has called for fuel storage tanks to be moved outside of the capital, Tehran, in order to protect civilians from new US or Israeli attacks, which US President Donald Trump is reportedly mulling over.
"The Crisis Management Organisation has issued a formal expert recommendation to relocate these tanks to safe sites outside the city in order to protect the lives and property of citizens," Hossein Sajedinia, the head of the organisation, was quoted as saying by Tasnim news agency.
Following renewed US troop movements into the Middle East, the US is reportedly gearing up for a new round of strikes on Iran after weeks of deliberations by President Donald Trump.
Trump has on several occasions stated that he would not launch new strikes until after the midterm elections, the latest being on Thursday, saying on Truth Social that discussions with Iran were "productive."
Yet, according to both The New York Times and Axios, Trump mulled the possibility of further strikes following a meeting with his national security staff in Camp David on 2 October. A final decision is set to occur within the next seven to 10 days, Israel's Channel 12 reported.
The New Arab explores if and how the US military will escalate tensions, and if Iran will retaliate.
The Saudi coalition has announced that it has struck 136 Houthi targets across Yemen as it continues to support the internationally recognised government.
Spokesperson for the coalition, Major General Turki al-Maliki, said that airstrikes aimed to destroy the Houthis ballistic missiles, which have been launched against Saudi Arabia, including energy facilities, alongside airports over the last week.
Israeli airstrikes have targeted an area between the towns of Nabatieh, al-Fawqa, and Kfar Tebnit, according to Lebanon's National News Agency. However, it is unknown whether there are any casualties.
Israeli forces have injured dozens of people, including a Palestinian journalist, during a raid on the occupied West Bank village of Deir Abu Mash'al, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.
Israeli forces shot journalist Issam al-Rimawi in the thigh with a rubber bullet, the agency reported, while others were injured after inhaling tear gas.
The raid came as soldiers attacked olive harvesters.

articles.title: More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
articles.body:
More than 50 Iranian army units deployed along borders, commander says
TEHRAN — Iran has deployed more than 50 combat and support units of its Army Ground Force along the country’s borders, including mobile, rapid-reaction, armored and mechanized brigades, as well as artillery, engineering, missile and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) units, the force’s commander has said.
Brigadier General Ali Jahanshahi, commander of the Islamic Republic of Iran Army Ground Force, said the force had revised its operational plans, restructured elements of its combat organization and strengthened its readiness in response to lessons learned from previous conflicts, including the 12-day war and the conflict Iranian officials refer to as the Ramadan War.
In remarks reported by Mehr News Agency, Jahanshahi said the post-war reforms had prioritized the introduction of precision-strike, smart and network-enabled weapons systems, alongside expanded training programs to enhance personnel proficiency and operational effectiveness.
 
He added that measures to reduce personnel casualties, protect military assets and sustain operational readiness included the construction of extensive tunnel networks, trenches, firing positions and defensive fortifications at military installations.
Large-scale force deployment across Iran
Jahanshahi said that, following the outbreak of the Ramadan War, more than 50 combat and support units had been deployed to border areas across the country.
The deployments extended from Iran’s northwestern and western frontiers to the southwest, east and southeast, as well as the Makran coastline. According to the commander, the redeployment effort involved more than nine million kilometers of road movements, alongside the transport of substantial quantities of ammunition and military equipment by heavy vehicles.
He said the movements were conducted under the surveillance and potential threat of hostile drones and aircraft, with forces repositioned at night to reduce their exposure. Jahanshahi said the deployment had strengthened Iran’s deterrence posture and helped prevent enemy forces from crossing the country’s borders.
He added that Ground Force units remained deployed along the frontiers and maintained operational readiness despite temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius, high humidity and limited logistical facilities.
ounter-infiltration measures and continued weapons production
Jahanshahi said military planners had identified locations that could potentially be used by hostile forces to enter Iranian territory, including disused airfields. Countermeasures had been planned for potential incursions, while intelligence operations had been conducted to improve situational awareness.
He also said domestic military production had continued throughout the conflict and remained ongoing.
According to Jahanshahi, the Army Ground Force, operating alongside other branches of Iran’s armed forces, launched thousands of Arash drones against US military bases in regional countries and targets associated with Israel during the war.
Passive defense measures limit personnel losses
The commander said several Ground Force installations had been struck during the conflict, with military buildings and personnel accommodation among the targets. At one base, he said, 10 barracks buildings were hit. Attacks also caused extensive damage to military infrastructure, destroying hundreds of thousands of square meters of buildings, according to his account.
Jahanshahi attributed the comparatively limited loss of life to the dispersal of personnel and the implementation of passive defense measures. Without those precautions, he said, the number of fatalities could have reached thousands.
Despite the damage, he added, personnel had maintained their positions and continued their missions.
Jahanshahi concluded that the Ground Force’s operational readiness and capabilities had improved significantly compared with the period before the conflict, with equipment production continuing and units maintaining their preparedness for potential threats.

articles.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die
articles.body:
Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.
The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.
By September, he had started to feel better and was on another work trip, this time to Poland. Asleep in his Warsaw hotel room, he was again woken by terrifying head pain, even worse than in London. He later described the sensation as “someone standing over me with a baseball bat and just repeatedly hitting me on the head”. It was a nine or 10 on the pain scale, he felt, worse than anything he could remember.
Two hours later, the same feeling returned, and he started to suspect that what was happening might not be an internal process but rather some external attack. He dragged himself off the bed and curled up on the floor, where the intense pain subsided somewhat. That was the last time he had the “attack” sensation, but he went on to suffer chronic nerve pain, fatigue and other severe health problems for years.
Sources described the man in question as a senior CIA officer who had recently been assigned an important job relating to worldwide operations against Russia. At the time, he was only vaguely aware of the stories that had emerged from Cuba two years previously, about US diplomats who believed they may have been attacked with a sonic weapon.
These incidents, in which people reported feeling a variety of unusual sounds, pressure and pain, followed by residual symptoms that could last for years, had acquired the name Havana syndrome, after the city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged.
Later, dozens of CIA officers around the world reported Havana syndrome episodes, which in official documents were called anomalous health incidents (AHIs). Many believed AHIs were the result of a Russian intelligence operation to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivered sonic or pulsed microwave energy.
There was sustained pushback against that theory. Some scientists insisted the idea of a portable weapon that could deliver these injuries belonged in the realm of science fiction. They said a whole range of conditions could cause pain, dizziness and cognitive issues.
Various experts suggested AHIs could be down to environmental factors, toxins or even the sound of chirping crickets. One explanation was that the symptoms were psychogenic and the result of “mass hysteria”, while some inside the CIA even accused those involved of faking their injuries in the hope of a medical payout. The disagreements over what was causing Havana syndrome led to bitter arguments and broken friendships at the spy agency.
In 2022, a panel of scientific experts convened by the US government concluded that “the signs and symptoms of AHIs are genuine and compelling” and “could be due to external stimuli”.
But the next year, a long-awaited report delivered the official assessment of the US intelligence community: “The available intelligence consistently points against the involvement of US adversaries in causing the reported incidents,” read an unclassified summary. It was “very unlikely” that a sinister Russian campaign was behind AHIs, it concluded.
Yet the mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die. This summer, the “very unlikely” assessment from 2023 was rescinded by Donald Trump’s outgoing director of national intelligence, who claimed it was based on flawed analysis.
Now, a decade after the first reports emerged from Havana, two CBS journalists who have covered the story from the start are to release a book that sets out the case for Russia being behind at least some of the episodes. It also accuses parts of the US government and intelligence community of covering up the evidence.
This article is based on early access to their findings, as well as on the Guardian’s own interviews with intelligence sources, AHI patients and scientists.
David Relman, the Stanford professor who led the official scientific panel on Havana syndrome in 2022, told the Guardian he believed there was a subset of AHI cases that were “most plausibly explained by exposure to pulsed microwave energy”.
His panel had access to patient records and to more than 1,000 classified documents on the topic. “To any reasonable person looking at all the evidence I was able to see, it inevitably leads to the conclusion that there may have been a cover-up,” he said.
Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados are longstanding producers for the CBS programme 60 Minutes. In an interview at the programme’s studios in midtown Manhattan, the pair recounted how they first came across the story a decade ago.
They covered the Obama administration’s policy of re-establishing diplomatic relations with Cuba in 2015, so when reports emerged the next year of a mysterious new condition afflicting employees at the reopened embassy in Havana, they contacted a senior US diplomat who had been posted there. “I expected him to say: ‘This is all bullshit,’” said Zill. “But he said: ‘Oh no, this is completely true. And I can put you in touch with a bunch of people who were hit.’”
The pair spoke to more than a dozen of them, off the record, but by the time they were ready to put a story together there were new reports of similar cases occurring among US diplomats stationed in China. Then there were whispers about it happening in other locations around the world.
Once the first 60 Minutes episodes devoted to the topic aired, victims started contacting the producers, keen to tell their stories. Many of these new sources were – or had been – undercover operatives for the CIA, meaning they could not speak openly as most details of their work were classified. But people stationed around the world who had not known each other told stories that seemed remarkably similar.
A pattern linked some of the key cases: the alleged victims were working, or had previously worked, on beats where they rubbed up against Russian interests.
In some cases, the location of the supposed hits was notable in itself: allies of Moscow where some part of the elite was looking to improve relations with the west. This was the case in Cuba, where the original cluster of cases had come during the Obama-era thaw in relations with the US, which had irritated hardliners in the Cuban regime and their backers in Moscow.
It was also the case in Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia and Vietnam. Several CIA officers who had been stationed in Kyiv around the time of the 2014 Maidan revolution in Ukraine, decried by the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as a US-backed coup, later suffered AHIs in different locations across the world.
“I went through years of doubts about the story, and all the crazy things we were hearing,” said Zill. But the more source meetings she and Rey had, the more they felt there really was something there. “We’re meeting these highly effective intelligence officers and they’re all telling versions of the same story,” said Rey.
The origins of Havana syndrome go back long before Cuba. A cornerstone case is that of Mike Beck, a counter-intelligence officer at the National Security Agency who got sick while on temporary assignment to an undisclosed location in the 1990s to check a US diplomatic facility for bugs.
Beck developed a rare form of Parkinson’s disease at the age of 45 and died this year. A declassified NSA statement, included in his 2014 workplace compensation claim, noted that “there is intelligence information from 2012 associating the hostile country to which Mr Beck travelled in the late 1990s with a high-powered microwave system weapon that may have the ability to weaken, intimidate or kill an enemy, over time, and without leaving evidence”. The unnamed “hostile country”, sources said, was Russia.
The first known AHIs among the contemporary batch of cases occurred in late 2014, when several US government employees at the consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, became ill. One was found unconscious in a consulate stairwell after feeling sudden, intense pressure on her chest and hearing a “high-pitched squeal”, Rey and Zill reported.
The next year, a researcher at a US defence institute – who asked the Guardian not to use her name – was on a tour of the Balkans, attending meetings with military officers from the host nations alongside US defence attaches. Her itinerary took in Montenegro, which was in the process of applying for Nato membership, and Serbia, a Russian ally that harboured resentments towards the US over the 1999 Nato bombing of Yugoslavia.
On her final evening in Belgrade, as she walked through lively pedestrianised streets to her hotel, the researcher was sure she spotted someone following her. Later, as she approached her hotel room, she felt “a sinking feeling, as though I was in a lift that was descending suddenly”, she recalled in a telephone interview.
Inside her room, she continued to feel odd sensations. “I just had this falling sensation, a feeling of gravity pulling at me, and nausea.” At one point, she turned on her government laptop and found the screen was flickering with blue static. The computer never worked again.
She said she was able to continue her trip, but in the subsequent weeks she felt weak, had difficulty speaking clearly and developed pain that felt “like a drill was going into my eye”. She was unable to focus at work. “I used up all my vacation, then my sick leave, then colleagues donated their leave. Eventually, I had to leave my job,” she said. It was only much later that she connected what had happened to her with reports about Havana syndrome.
The next cohort of AHI patients included people at the heart of a new CIA policy on Russia. In 2017, as Donald Trump took office for the first time, the agency launched a drive to push back against the increasingly brazen global reach of Moscow’s intelligence agencies.
“They wanted us to take the same kind of tactics and spirit we used in the global war on terror to the Russians,” said Marc Polymeropoulos, who was made deputy chief of operations for Europe and Eurasia in 2017. Polymeropoulos, who had spent most of his career in the Middle East, was one of several veterans of the “war on terror” who were moved to senior roles focused on Russia. Even as Trump publicly denied that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, the agency made plans to push back hard against Russian activity.
“Obviously, we didn’t have permission to run lethal operations against the Russians, but we could do things we hadn’t done as much previously, such as enlist the help of multiple friendly services and expose the Russians for what they were doing,” said Polymeropoulos, in an interview at a restaurant just outside Washington.
In early December 2017, Polymeropoulos and another senior CIA executive made a liaison trip to Moscow, to meet their counterparts in Russia’s SVR and FSB intelligence services. The official meetings were ill-tempered and lacking in substance. Late one night, Polymeropoulos woke up suddenly in his hotel room. “I had vertigo and a splitting headache. I thought it was food poisoning at first, I thought I was going to puke and crap my brains out, and I remember being like, holy shit, the room is spinning and my ears are ringing,” he said.
On his return to Washington, Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside, and with superiors who insisted his symptoms were unrelated to other AHIs. He saw a variety of doctors on his own time, but owing to the classified nature of his job he could not share details of where he had been when he became ill.
He left the CIA in 2019 and, frustrated at being stonewalled in his requests for medical assessment, became the first CIA officer to go public with a Havana syndrome story under their real name, telling the journalist Julia Ioffe about what happened in Moscow.
The resulting publicity prompted the CIA to send him to the Walter Reed military medical centre, where he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. In 2023 he was found eligible for compensation under the Havana Act, which authorised payments to “personnel who incur brain injuries from hostilities while on assignment”. The financial payout was modest, but he saw it as a moral victory after years of fighting for recognition.
One early theory was that AHIs could be the result of data collection attempts gone wrong – a machine designed to pull classified data from operatives’ electronic devices that had unfortunate side-effects when turned up too high. That is still seen by some as a possibility, although even if intelligence collection was the initial idea, the damaging health effects would have quickly become apparent to the operators.
Some observers insisted the whole concept of “Havana syndrome” was an invention. They asked why, if Russia possessed a brain-frying weapon, it was not using it on a wider range of its enemies. Why were there not more reports of collateral victims?
The sociologist Robert Bartholomew and the neurologist Robert Baloh co-authored a book that declared the whole story a hoax – “a case study in the social construction of mass psychogenic illness” – borne of high-stress work environments and propagated by excitable journalists.
Douglas Fields, a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claimed in a journal article that the medical studies of patients which showed cognitive changes had used unsound methodology, and that theories of an energy weapon “defy the laws of physics”. Reports of Havana syndrome should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster, he suggested.
Other scientists, including some who had reviewed patients’ medical records, strongly disagreed. “The early scepticism was perfectly appropriate, but over time we started to see an increase in the number of individuals who have gone through clinical evaluations that cannot be faked,” said James Giordano, a professor emeritus of neurology at Georgetown University Medical Center and the forensic neuroscientist on the original cohort of cases from Havana.
“We are talking about objective signs that are presenting with a very distinct pattern,” Giordano said. Key symptoms included “a profound tumbling or falling sensation” as well as pressure in the head, chest and throat, and cognitive effects. It was true that chemical or drug exposure could cause similar symptoms, he said, but this would be visible on blood tests. Another key factor was the sudden onset and the sense of a specific location where the apparent attack felt strongest.
When the Biden administration took office in 2021, the then CIA director, Bill Burns, and the director of national intelligence, Avril Haines, vowed to get to the bottom of the issue. Burns met many of the AHI cohort, including Polymeropoulos, listening carefully to their stories and promising them a full investigation.
Burns also fired the CIA’s chief medical officer, who had infuriated some AHI patients by accusing them of faking their symptoms. The same year, more than 100 CIA operatives and other US government officials reported AHIs in locations around the world. In Vienna, there were so many hits that the work of the CIA station was essentially paralysed and the station chief recalled. A spate of government employees also reported incidents on US soil, including several who claimed to have been hit on the grounds of the White House. Was this an adversary stepping up its campaign, or was the increasing publicity about AHIs leading more people to misidentify other conditions or episodes as Havana syndrome?
Burns and Haines launched two investigations, one to re-examine intelligence on whether a foreign adversary was behind Havana syndrome, and another that convened a panel of scientists and physicians to determine whether it was even possible for a weapon to cause the symptoms.
Relman, a Stanford professor who chaired the scientific panel, said its members were given access to open source and classified scientific studies into pulsed radio frequency energy, which suggested that the science behind there being a “device” that could cause AHI symptoms was plausible. Scientists who disagreed were simply unaware of the research into such technology that had been taking place for decades in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and then Russia, he said.
Regarding the medical results, Relman conceded that plenty – perhaps the vast majority – of AHI claims could be explained by other factors. But there were dozens of cases “that were unusual in the distinctness of their features and the near impossibility of explaining them based on known medical and environmental conditions”. In short: the publicity around AHIs may have prompted a wave of false reporting, but a core subset of cases seemed real.
Determining who may have carried out such attacks was beyond Relman’s purview. That fell to the second expert group, which in 2023 issued the assessment that it was “very unlikely” to be caused by a foreign adversary, dismaying many AHI patients who had hoped to finally receive closure on what caused their health problems.
Even people who have seen the intelligence on Havana syndrome can disagree on what it suggests. Two sources offered the Guardian radically different interpretations of what the classified data shows on possible Russian involvement.
One highlighted the lack of a “smoking gun”; a piece of human intelligence or an intercept that showed Russian operatives discussing a programme to use directed energy against Americans.
“Everyone has seen how strong our collection capabilities on Russia are,” the source said, referencing how US intelligence got hold of Putin’s war plans before his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “If this was really a large-scale Russian programme, we would have expected to see something in some of these channels, but we didn’t.”
Another former intelligence official disagreed: “If you’re waiting for an intercept of someone saying: ‘My name is Igor and I’m going to press the button on my secret laser’ before you have confidence, that’s probably never going to happen. But for any reasonable person who has access to the intelligence and knows how to read it, the Russian fingerprints are clear.”
If that is the case, it raises the question of why the 2023 intelligence community assessment found it “very unlikely” that a foreign actor was involved. At the end of the Biden administration, a tweaked version said that while five US intelligence agencies still found it “very unlikely”, one agency now believed there was a “roughly even chance” that a foreign actor had used “a novel weapon or prototype device” in a number of attacks.
This summer, both of those Biden-era assessments were rescinded by Trump’s director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in a memo issued just before she left office. Gabbard said the earlier assessments were marred by “selective exclusion of evidence” and “mischaracterisation of sources”, though the statement did not release any new evidence or provide a revised assessment.
While Gabbard had a chequered reputation among the intelligence community, Mark Zaid, a lawyer who represents more than 30 AHI patients, welcomed her memo and said it was a first step to overturning a CIA cover-up. When asked why the CIA might have perpetrated such a cover-up, Zaid suggested it could be to protect its reputation after prior negligence. “This has built up to a level that the agency can’t let the truth get out because it’s going to reflect so poorly on them,” he said.
Burns, in a comment for Rey and Zill’s book, said it was “simply not true that there was a ‘cover-up’ by the CIA” and described the earlier investigation as “a rigorous effort across the entire intelligence community”.
Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. “There’s not a single cigar-filled backroom meeting that led to decisions getting made,” said Rey. “There was a lot of, ‘This is a pain in the ass’ or ‘The president’s not going to want to hear this’. There was bureaucratic dysfunction, careerism and things that just got in the way of proper investigation.”
One example he gave is the fact that the FBI sent criminal investigators, rather than counterintelligence investigators with access to classified information, to Havana after the attacks there. Another is a nascent investigation at CIA headquarters in late 2019 which reportedly found that, in some cases, phones linked to Russian intelligence operatives had been in the vicinity of suspected Havana syndrome incidents. These included the hits that year on the senior CIA officer in London and Warsaw.
In London, a suspicious phone had supposedly been just 10 metres (30ft) away from his hotel room. But when the then CIA director, Gina Haspel, was briefed on these findings, she allegedly complained it was not solid enough to take to the president, given how sensitive he was on Russia-related matters. “The meeting abruptly ended after Haspel shouted that if she took reports like this to President Trump, she would be fired as director,” Rey and Zill write.
Outside the CIA, some have uncovered intriguing leads about possible links between Russian operatives and AHIs. Christo Grozev, a journalist and investigator who has exposed several Russian intelligence operations, claimed leaked travel data suggested at least four potential crossovers between suspected AHIs and travel by officers from Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence, known for its campaign of sabotage and assassinations in western countries. He also said he had traced travel by “members of what appears to be a technical unit adjacent to 29155” to Cuba during the initial attacks.
Perhaps the most significant piece of evidence to emerge recently has been the alleged US government acquisition of a “Havana syndrome-style device” in an undercover operation. First reported by the independent journalist Sasha Ingber this year, two sources confirmed to the Guardian that a device had been acquired and brought to the US in late 2024 for testing, after a purchase from a dark-web seller.
Rey and Zill’s book recounts a meeting with a person who claimed to be part of the undercover team that acquired the device. The source told them the device was “man-portable”, shot non-thermal pulsed microwaves and was acquired from “a complex Russian illicit network”.
It was not believed to have been used in a Havana syndrome incident, but testing on animals has reportedly shown it may cause similar symptoms to AHIs, which could prove that building such a device is scientifically possible.
That would make the case for a weapon being involved in some incidents more plausible, and would also raise new and worrying questions. If such weapons have proliferated to the extent that one can be bought on the dark web, how many devices could be out there and who may have access to them? Could AHIs thus have not one perpetrator, but many? And is there a future in which such weapons become a widespread element of warfare? “We know the technology has reached a level that enables it to be used in weaponisable ways,” said Giordano. “I see that as a clear and present threat.”
For those who have had symptoms for years, the acquisition of the device and the rescinded intelligence assessments provide some hope that, one day, they will receive official confirmation that they were targeted by a foreign adversary. For many of them, the lack of recognition at home has angered them more than the attack itself.
“The Russians are our enemy, I put them in the same bucket as al-Qaida or the Taliban, or any other groups I worked against,” said Polymeropoulos. “Do I want to see them held accountable? Of course. But I’m actually more upset and feel more of a betrayal from my own government.”
- The Havana Syndrome by Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados is published by Crown Publishing in the US on 13 October and by WH Allen in the UK on 15 October.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukrainian Peace Team in Florida Used as ‘Smokescreen’ for US-Russia Diesel Deal
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky delivered a blistering rebuke of Washington on Friday, Oct. 9, after US President Donald Trump struck a separate energy deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin while Ukrainian peace negotiators were in Florida – handing Moscow a massive financial lifeline to sustain its invasion.
The diplomatic contrast could hardly have been sharper. As Ukrainian officials sat down with their US counterparts in Miami to explore ways to halt Russia’s war, Trump spoke directly with the man who launched it, agreeing to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The arrangement stands to generate substantial new revenue for Moscow at a time when Ukraine and its European partners have been pressing for maximum economic pressure to cripple the Kremlin’s war machine.
Speaking to journalists Friday evening, Zelensky sharply questioned Washington’s approach, challenging how the US could credibly mediate peace while simultaneously offering Putin sudden economic relief.
Ukraine seeks ceasefire as Trump cuts deal with Moscow
According to President Zelensky, Ukraine’s negotiating team traveled to Florida to seek a pathway toward ending Russia’s full-scale invasion – or, at the very least, securing an initial ceasefire.
“Right now, our Ukrainian team, our negotiating team, is in Florida, holding talks with the American team about ending this terrible war – or, at the very least, achieving a ceasefire,” Zelensky said.
Trump Names Truth Social Adviser Katie Zacharia as New White House Press Secretary
He emphasized that an agreement to halt attacks on energy infrastructure could provide an urgent first step toward a broader de-escalation, particularly as relentless Russian strikes threaten Ukrainian homes, the power grid, and essential services ahead of winter.
“An energy ceasefire could be the first step toward a broader ceasefire. This is extremely important for our people, for our families.”
The high-level Ukrainian delegation in Florida includes Presidential Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Rustem Umerov, First Deputy Chief of Staff Serhiy Kyslytsia, and parliamentary faction leader Davyd Arakhamia. They have been holding talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, alongside representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the EU, and NATO.
But as those sensitive negotiations unfolded in Miami, Trump was pursuing an entirely different conversation with the Kremlin.
“At this very moment, while our team is talking with the American team in Florida, the president of the United States is having a conversation with the Kremlin leader – the leader of this war, the leader of this aggression,” Zelensky stated. “And they reach an agreement under which America allows Russia to export diesel.”
For Ukraine, the decision risks undermining one of the West’s most critical tools for pressuring Putin to end the war.
‘Additional money for this war against us’
Trump defended the arrangement in a post on his social media platform, Truth Social, announcing that Russia had agreed to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November and 1 million tons afterward.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would deliver another 3 million tons of diesel within a short period, depending on the operational condition of its refineries.
Combined with what Trump termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the US president claimed the agreement would rapidly lower domestic fuel costs.
Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued General License 135, officially authorizing transactions involving the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sudden authorization came just three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18 – legislation explicitly designed to choke off Russia’s energy revenues and financial networks. Bipartisan US lawmakers had strongly urged Washington to fully implement the law ahead of its mid-October deadlines, warning that the Kremlin was exploiting loopholes to keep bankrolling its front lines.
Zelensky warned that the financial windfall from lifting these sanctions is impossible to separate from the violence on the ground.
“This is additional money, additional money for this war against us, without question,” the Ukrainian president said. “It only fuels Putin and gives him the opportunity to wage even more war.”
“And at this very moment, when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel,” Zelensky continued. “I don’t know whether we’re talking about millions or billions. In any case, all of it goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us.”
US fuel prices prioritized over sanctions pressure
The White House has framed the deal as a pragmatic response to severe domestic economic pressures. US diesel prices have recently climbed to an average of approximately $6.28 per gallon, squeezing truck drivers, agricultural supply chains, and American consumers.
However, energy analysts and European allies note that the initial shipment of 300,000 tons is modest compared to total US daily consumption, raising doubts about whether the deal can deliver the sweeping price relief Trump promised.
Furthermore, the decision risks severely fracturing the unified Western sanctions strategy.
For nearly five years, the US and its allies have sought to starve Moscow of the energy revenues required to pay military salaries, manufacture missiles, and sustain its occupation.
Allowing Russian diesel back into Western-regulated markets effectively rewards the Kremlin without securing any corresponding concession, such as a halt to attacks on Ukrainian civilians.
‘Gifts to Putin will not bring peace’
Zelensky reinforced his criticism in a separate statement on X, describing the sudden easing of energy sanctions as an investment in prolonging the war rather than ending it.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world,” Zelensky wrote.
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky was even more direct, calling the arrangement “not fair and not honest,” likening it to a birthday present for Putin, who turned 74 earlier this week.
Zelensky concluded his remarks to journalists by returning to what he characterized as the fundamentally unfair treatment of Ukraine’s negotiating team.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said. “And that is definitely unfair. It is definitely not how partners should behave.”
“And it is a weak decision. Unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners. Glory to Ukraine!”

articles.title: Trump pressured Ukraine to unilaterally halt strikes on Russian oil refineries – Axios
articles.body:
Trump pressured Ukraine to unilaterally halt strikes on Russian oil refineries – Axios
Axios reported this, citing a U.S. official familiar with the situation, Ukrinform says.
According to the report, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have been highly effective in recent months, triggering an energy crisis in Russia. In response, Russia banned diesel fuel exports, increasing pressure on global markets already facing disruptions caused by the war in Iran.
Zelensky told Trump and his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, that Ukraine was ready to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia, for its part, stopped attacking Ukrainian power plants.
According to the U.S. official, Trump insisted that Ukraine halt the strikes unilaterally because they were contributing to higher gasoline prices in the United States. At the same time, the White House chief did not consider strikes on Russian oil refineries equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“President Trump decided to make a diesel fuel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries,” the source told Axios.
In an interview with Axios following the announcement of the deal, Zelensky said it came as a surprise to him. The Ukrainian President called it “not fair and not honest” and an unjustified gift to Putin, according to the publication.
The report says that during eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainian delegation that Trump planned to speak with Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports after Ukraine ignored repeated requests to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries, which had a direct impact on American consumers.
The publication notes that, according to a Ukrainian official, Witkoff and Kushner “threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests.”
At the same time, a U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner emphasized that the United States was a reliable partner providing Ukraine with ammunition and intelligence, and that Kyiv should therefore refrain from actions that harm American consumers.
During the talks, Witkoff and Kushner presented a package of measures for Ukraine’s postwar period. It included mechanisms to finance the country’s reconstruction and military development, as well as proposals to cover the budget deficit caused by the war. The participants also discussed a roadmap for Ukraine’s accession to the EU and Kyiv’s future relations with NATO after the war.
In addition, Witkoff and Kushner raised the possibility of creating a postwar security system between Europe and Russia that would satisfy both sides.
The U.S. mediators briefed Ukrainian and European representatives on possible energy deals with Russia. According to the official, Washington hopes these agreements will help lower energy prices and encourage Moscow to make concessions in peace talks.
The source told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner were considering visiting Moscow and Kyiv next week to discuss peace proposals. However, it remains unclear how the dispute that arose on Friday will affect their plans.
“Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop,” the U.S. official said.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 9, U.S. President Donald Trump said that Russia, with U.S. approval, would supply 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the global market and significantly increase its exports going forward.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that gifts to Putin would not contribute to peace or benefit the civilized world, warning that Russia would “repay” them with further terror and treachery.

articles.title: Putin and Trump hold phone talks – Kremlin
articles.body:
Putin and Trump hold ‘successful’ talks: Key details
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump held a 90-minute phone conversation on Friday, discussing the Ukraine conflict, a major agreement on Russian diesel supplies, the crisis surrounding Iran, and prospects for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington.
Trump described the exchange as “highly successful,” announcing that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to ease soaring energy prices.
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the conversation was friendly and substantive, revealing that Trump had rearranged his schedule to speak with Putin following the Russian leader’s 74th birthday.
Here are the key takeaways from the conversation, according to statements by both leaders and the Kremlin’s detailed readout.
Millions of tons of Russian diesel for the US
The most immediate result of the talks was a major energy agreement under which Russia will increase diesel exports to the US and global markets, potentially helping alleviate an international fuel shortage.
Trump announced that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons shortly thereafter. He also suggested that Russia could deliver an additional 3 million tons, depending on the condition of its refineries.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak subsequently confirmed that Moscow would begin lifting its diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, reiterating the announced volumes and clarifying that exports could eventually reach 3 million tons per month, while assuring that Russia’s domestic market would remain fully supplied.
The US Treasury also issued a temporary sanctions waiver covering Russian diesel shipments until April 7, 2027.
Trump predicted that the agreement, together with Washington’s claimed control of the Strait of Hormuz, would bring diesel prices down rapidly, particularly benefiting American farmers, truckers and consumers.
Kiev ‘derailed’ peace talks
The Ukraine conflict dominated much of the discussion, with Putin briefing Trump on the situation along the front line and Moscow’s response to Ukrainian “terrorist strikes” on infrastructure and civilian targets deep inside Russian territory. The Russian leader stressed that Moscow retained the initiative and remained committed to its objectives, while expressing readiness for a lasting diplomatic settlement.
However, Putin said that Kiev had effectively sabotaged plans for the immediate resumption of trilateral negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States. During their previous conversation, the two leaders had discussed restarting the talks shortly after Russia’s State Duma elections. Ushakov said that Ukrainian drone attacks, including strikes targeting polling stations and election-related personnel, had fundamentally changed the situation.
Moscow would now reconsider when negotiations could resume, according to the Kremlin aide. Trump reportedly promised to convey Russia’s position to Ukrainian representatives meeting with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami.
Iran diplomacy ‘not exhausted’
Putin stressed that a negotiated settlement with Tehran remained possible, citing his October 8 meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan.
According to Ushakov, Putin noted that Washington and Tehran continued indirect contacts through Qatar despite their confrontational rhetoric.
Moscow also reiterated its offer to accept highly enriched Iranian uranium as a potential way out of the nuclear deadlock. Trump welcomed Russia’s involvement in diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis, Ushakov added.
Melania’s humanitarian mission
Putin personally thanked First Lady Melania Trump for her efforts to reunite children separated from their families during the Ukraine conflict.
The leaders also discussed the humanitarian situation in the town of Aleshki in Russia’s Kherson Region, agreeing that Russian human rights official Yana Lantratova would maintain direct contact with Melania’s office.
Closer ties – and another summit?
The leaders expressed satisfaction with existing communication channels between their administrations, intelligence services and other government agencies, agreeing to maintain cooperation.
Putin emphasized that Moscow appreciated the attention Trump and his team continued to devote to relations with Russia despite Washington’s domestic and Middle Eastern priorities.
Asked whether the two presidents had agreed to meet in person, Ushakov said no specific summit had been discussed. However, he suggested that the upcoming APEC summit in China could provide an opportunity for another encounter if both leaders attended.
The Kremlin aide also declined to disclose whether Washington had offered any concessions in exchange for Russia’s agreement to supply diesel, suggesting that American officials might provide further clarification.
Birthday wishes and hockey diplomacy
The conversation was initially proposed by the American side as an opportunity for Trump to personally congratulate Putin on his October 7 birthday. According to Ushakov, Witkoff contacted the Kremlin that day to convey greetings from Trump, as well as personal wishes from himself and Kushner, who expressed hope of meeting the Russian leader again soon.
Officials subsequently arranged the call around Putin’s trip to Turkmenistan and the time difference between Moscow and Washington, with Trump postponing some previously scheduled engagements.
The US president opened the conversation with birthday wishes and greetings from Melania. The leaders also found time to discuss sports, with Trump praising Russian hockey star Alexander Ovechkin’s contribution to the game.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln Returns to USA With Markers Indicating Destroyed Iranian Targets: 103 Drones, 34 Ships, and 10 Submarines
articles.body:
The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned to the United States after a nearly 11-month deployment, during which its strike group participated in combat operations against Iran and destroyed dozens of ships, drones, and missiles.
This was reported by The War Zone, whose journalists analyzed photographs of the aircraft carrier after the conclusion of its combat deployment.
Markings in the form of silhouettes of destroyed targets have appeared on the ship’s superstructure. Journalists counted 103 markings for attack drones and 34 markings for ships and boats. The images of the drones resemble the Shahed-136, but may also represent other types of Iranian drones.
According to official data announced on October 7 by U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hagseth, during Operation Epic Fury, the carrier strike group shot down 77 attack drones, sank 64 Iranian vessels, and destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles.
These results cover the period from the start of Operation Epic Fury on February 28 until the carrier strike group’s departure from the region on August 22, 2026.
During this period, the group’s aircraft flew 3,693 combat sorties and expended approximately 621 metric tons of air-to-ground munitions. Escort ships also launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles at ground targets.
Specific markings on carrier-based fighter jets indicate the destruction of Iranian submarines. In particular, a corresponding image was recorded on an F/A-18F Super Hornet from the 41st Strike Fighter Squadron (VFA-41). In total, this squadron deployed 421 missiles and aerial bombs during combat operations.
At the same time, the number of marks on the aircraft carrier does not match official statistics.
On its superstructure, there were 26 more drone marks than indicated in the award document, but 30 fewer ship marks. The reasons for the discrepancies have not yet been explained.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln returned to San Diego on October 8 after more than 320 days of deployment. As part of the operation against Iran, its strike group received the Presidential Unit Citation for combat merit.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that on August 22, the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group left the Middle East after completing its combat deployment and moved into the area of responsibility of the U.S. 7th Fleet.
The extended deployment was accompanied by logistical challenges due to the threat of Iranian strikes on ports in the region.

articles.title: While Washington eases up on Russia, Europe hits back harder: EU plans to pass its largest sanctions package on Russia’s war machine in two days
articles.body:
Europe will not loosen its pressure on Russia after the US-Russia diesel deal, EU Foreign Policy chief Kaja Kallas says. She has announced that EU foreign ministers will approve the bloc’s largest set of sanctions against Russia’s war machine since the full-scale invasion on 12 October.
Washington has just eased the pressure on Russia, letting Russian diesel back onto world markets and handing Moscow more money to wage war. This comes as Russian strikes have killed more than 80 Ukrainian civilians in two days, 22 of them on Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday on 7 October.
Moreover, Russia has stepped up its hybrid attacks against Europe, both EU Member States and NATO Allies. It is now the time to tighten sanctions, not loosen them, Kallas says.
“Suspending sanctions on Russian diesel provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war. This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” she claims.
A split with Washington
On 9 October, Trump claimed he had agreed with Putin to put more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel on world markets immediately.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the deal a weak decision by strong partners, arguing that Russia turns oil-product revenue into weapons against Ukraine's civilians, according to the BBC.
The package aims at the missile chain
On 7 October, EU ambassadors approved the 22nd package of sanctions, with about 1,700 listings, Ukrainian President’s Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk notes. It is expected to be formally approved on 12 October. 
This package contains the largest number of sanctions targeting Russia’s defence industry. Of these, 60% were drawn from Ukrainian decrees and proposals. The package includes measures targeting machine tools, Lancet drones, ballistic weapons, and related technologies.
“The core of the package is Russia’s missile programme and electronic components: electronics, capacitors, resistors, and semiconductors. It also covers electronic warfare, shipbuilding, and explosives,” Vlasiuk says.
It took just a few weeks from Ukraine's decision to the European one.
"But we are already working on further measures, including sectoral sanctions targeting energy, the defense industry, finance, and trade,” he stated.

articles.title: Latvia’s Pro-Ukraine Landslide Hides a Weakness Putin Could Exploit
articles.body:
Latvia has just held what its own public broadcaster called “a bit of an embarrassing” election. This bashfulness from Latvia’s National Public Service Broadcaster, LSM, was because only 51.8% of eligible voters turned out, the lowest result since Latvia’s first parliamentary election in the modern era in 1993.
Yet those who did turn out handed Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs and his United List 35.3% of the vote and 42 of the 100 seats in the Saeima, Latvia’s parliament – the strongest result achieved by a single political force since Latvia regained independence.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Latvia has emerged from the election with an unusually strong government and an unusually disengaged electorate.
For most European democracies, that would primarily be a political problem. For Latvia, it is also a security problem.
Latvia is a NATO frontline state of just 1.8 million people, bordering both Russia and Belarus. Its grand strategy can be reduced to one overriding objective: make Latvia impossible to isolate.
Internationalize survival
Latvia cannot deter Russia through mass. It has to do it through connections. That means embedding NATO troops on Latvian soil, keeping the United States and Canada strategically invested in the Baltic region, and integrating more closely with Poland and the Nordic states.
It means spending close to 5% of GDP on defense, building fortifications along the eastern frontier, investing in drones and air defense, and reducing Russian economic and informational leverage.
Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
Above all, it means supporting Ukraine. For Riga, Ukraine is both an ally and a forward school of national defense. The Ukrainian battlefield provides lessons in drones, electronic warfare, air defense and Russian tactics that Latvia hopes never to have to learn for itself.
Kulbergs has received a powerful mandate to continue this Atlanticist course. A likely coalition with the National Alliance and New Unity would control 59 seats. Support for Ukraine and NATO remains firmly anchored at the center of the Latvian government.
But Latvia’s defense strategy also depends on something NATO cannot provide: a cohesive and politically engaged society.
                                                                                                                                                                         Barely half Latvia’s electorate voted, raising uncomfortable questions for a national defence strategy built partly around participation and social cohesion. (Photo: PAP/Abaca)                             
The internal front line
Latvia follows an all-of-society approach to defense. Its National Security Concept is explicit that “the existence of the State of Latvia depends on a responsible attitude of all inhabitants of Latvia towards the State and its security.” It links national resilience to the readiness of society as a whole, while defining internal security as resting on a “cohesive civil society” whose citizens participate actively and are prepared to contribute to the defense of the state in a crisis.
Defense Minister Raivis Melnis put it clearly just over a week before the election: “The real first thing is resilience, which is people and country resilience.”
Then almost half of Latvia’s electorate stayed at home. Low turnout does not mean half the country would refuse to defend Latvia. But it does expose weakness in some of the social foundations on which Latvia itself says national resilience depends.
President Edgars Rinkēvičs has already drawn attention to the danger. “Disappointment and indifference are dangerous to the democratic foundations and future of our country,” he said after the result.
Participation was particularly weak in parts of Latgale, Latvia’s easternmost and most heavily Russian-speaking region. Turnout in Daugavpils, where Russian is dominant in everyday life, was just 46.55%. This takes us to the most sensitive part of Latvia’s security dilemma.
Russian-speaking does not mean pro-Russian
Almost a quarter of Latvia’s population is ethnically Russian, while Russian is spoken at home by a much larger share. That demographic legacy of the Soviet period has long made Latvia different from Lithuania and has placed questions of language, history and identity close to the center of national politics.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the temptation has been to view this population primarily through the lens of security.
The evidence is considerably more complicated. Former Latvian integration minister Nils Muižnieks said: “I do not think that we can talk about a fifth column in Latvia.”
Research among Russian-speaking Latvians also suggests that straightforward support for Moscow is a minority position. One major study found 55% supporting neither Russia nor Ukraine. Researcher Mārtiņš Kaprāns argues that this “neutrality cannot be reduced to apathy or ignorance.”
                                                                                                                                                                         Latvia’s parliament has emerged with a stronger governing majority, but record-low turnout raises questions about political engagement beyond its walls. (Photo by Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)                             
The bigger problem appears to be alienation. Parts of Latvia’s Russian-speaking population have become detached from the country’s mainstream political and media environment. Some distrust Riga.
Some dislike policies reducing the public role of the Russian language. Some have become politically homeless following the collapse of Harmony, the party that once dominated Russian-speaking politics.
This election suggests that the two responses to that alienation are abstention and protest voting. Latvia First and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians, both considerably softer towards Moscow than the governing parties, will together control 32 seats.
That does not turn their voters into Kremlin loyalists. But from the perspective of national resilience, alienation is important.
The next stage of Latvian security
Russia does not need Latvia’s Russian speakers to become a fifth column. A population that distrusts state institutions, withdraws from politics or feels that the Latvian state belongs to somebody else already creates a seam Moscow can exploit.
Latvia therefore faces a difficult balancing act. It has good reason to restrict Russian influence, dismantle the remnants of Soviet political power and protect Latvian as the language of the state. At the same time, successful resilience ultimately requires Russian-speaking citizens to feel that they have ownership of that state too.
Latvia has spent years hardening its borders, strengthening its military and embedding itself so deeply inside NATO that Moscow could never confront it alone.
Kulbergs’s landslide gives him an unusually strong mandate to continue that work. The embarrassing part of this election is the reminder that Latvia’s next line of defense has to be built from citizens who believe strongly enough in the Latvian state to participate in it.

articles.title: US Democrats call on FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel upcoming trip to Russia
articles.body:
Two top House Democrats are urging FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel a reported trip to Russia, warning in an Oct. 9 letter that the visit could pose security risks.
Politico first reported in July that Patel was planning a fall visit to Russia, where he will be hosted by Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). He is allegedly set to visit both Moscow and St. Petersburg during the trip, which is tentatively scheduled for Oct. 14.
In the letter, Rep. Jamie Raskin and Rep. Jim Himes urged the FBI director to cancel the trip, citing “urgent national security concerns,” including the FSB's history of conducting espionage operations against American officials.
Rep. Jamie Raskin is a Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee and Rep. Himes is a Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The Democrats refer to Russia as a "hostile foreign power" and question why the FBI Director would visit a country that "has been committing war crimes, conducting influence operations against U.S. elections, conducting malicious cyberattacks against our critical infrastructure, and helping our adversaries target and kill American soldiers?"
read also
The letter described the visit as part of the FBI’s expanded cooperation with Russian and Chinese law enforcement agencies, citing Reuters reports that Patel has forged new partnerships with agencies in both countries.
In their letter to Patel, officials also question the timing of the FBI director's visit, citing the sanctions bill signed by President Trump which targets Russia's economy over its war against Ukraine.
Yet, on the same day the letter was published, Trump announced that Russia would supply U.S. and global markets with millions of tons of Russian diesel.
"This is why I voted against the Russia sanctions bill," Rep. Himes wrote on social media on Oct. 9. "Trump was never going to sanction Russia. He's going to refill Putin’s coffers and get an oil deal done to enrich his cronies."
The FBI has not replied to the letter or confirmed Patel's travel plans.
Since taking over the bureau in February 2025, Patel has sought closer ties with Moscow. This has raised concerns within the FBI, given the Kremlin's history of aggressive intelligence operations against the United States, according to an Oct. 9 investigation by The Atlantic.
Patel has previously called on Congress to investigate how U.S. aid to Ukraine is being used, and has criticized the amount of aid being sent.
The Trump appointee has also taken money from pro-Kremlin operatives in the past, according to the Washington Post. Patel received $25,000 in 2024 from a film company run by pro-Kremlin filmmaker Igor Lopatonok, the WP reported in Feb. 2025.
While the role of FBI director has traditionally been considered independent from government influence, U.S. national security expert Evelyn Farkas has described Patel as one of Trump's "yes men."

articles.title: In three years, Israel's war on Gaza hasn't just changed the Middle East, it's changed the world | Steve Bloomfield
articles.body:
There was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, for Israel, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.
The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps, released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.
For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with which Hamas carried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.
Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition. But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.
Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.
The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan and a fresh conflict inside Ethiopia.
More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.
But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.
We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.
Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.
All of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire was vetoed, and Biden who attacked the international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.
US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.
Ronald Reagan suspended an arms deal in 1981 after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administration stopped supplying cluster weapons to Israel after Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, to announce a review of Israel’s use of American arms.
Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.
Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.
The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.
Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness to accurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing” indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.
In the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.
Nor should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.
In Tigray, the northernmost part of Ethiopia, a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.
Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.
And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a daily deadly gamble. A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.
And in Gaza, crammed into tents, deprived of enough food and water, two million Palestinians are still living under the brutal rule of Hamas and the daily threat of death from a military force that fears no consequences.
This is our world now. We need to recognise that, if anything is going to change.
- Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer
