articles.title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and his shadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.
In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. He reminds us that in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous country for Europe.
Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former. So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK) has now given more aid to Ukraine than the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.
And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to the Kiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France. As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defence systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defence batteries – two more than the US itself has given.
In the first year of this war, I argued that Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is. This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defence spending, which, on the latest projections from the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same as Russia’s total estimated military expenditure for this year).
It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking the train from Germany to Ukraine on the evening of 3 October, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defence industry leaders. The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.
For a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’s Germany and Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it. In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.
Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty of Ukraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.
But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, from explosive-laden drones at Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia and assassination threats against defence industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation. While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.
A sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine. Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italian opinion poll last month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.
In Brussels recently, I found a large audience seemingly stalwart in support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter … Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.
Putin believes decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.
- Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book, Europe in 7½ Chapters, is published next week

articles.title: Turkish F-16s help guard Latvia’s skies during election
articles.body:
- Turkish Air Force F-16s completed a short deployment to Latvia’s Lielvārde Air Base to support NATO air defense during Latvia’s parliamentary elections.
- Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis visited the Turkish unit on Oct. 9 to thank it; Germany and Italy also sent jets.
Turkish Air Force F-16 fighter jets have completed a short deployment to Latvia’s Lielvārde Air Base, where they helped guard the country’s airspace around its parliamentary elections, Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis said on Oct. 9.
Melnis visited the Turkish unit at the base on Friday to thank it for the deployment. The Latvian Ministry of Defense said the F-16s were in the country temporarily to support NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defence mission, the alliance’s standing system for protecting member states’ airspace. The ministry did not say how many jets took part, how long they stayed or whether they were scrambled to intercept anything during their stay. Photos released with the visit show F-16s from the Turkish Air Force’s 181st Squadron.
“I thank Türkiye for its responsiveness and quick action in making a significant contribution to strengthening the security of Latvia’s airspace. The presence of Turkish fighter jets in Lielvārde demonstrates NATO’s ability to react quickly and effectively move forces where they are needed. Close allied cooperation, mutual trust and readiness to act together are an essential prerequisite for the security of Latvia and NATO’s entire eastern flank,” said Melnis.
Latvia, like Estonia and Lithuania, has no fighter jets of its own. NATO has protected Baltic skies since 2004 through its Baltic Air Policing mission, which normally bases allied fighters at Šiauliai in Lithuania and Ämari in Estonia. Latvia usually does not host permanently stationed jets, so the ministry said the Turkish deployment also tested how quickly NATO can move aircraft into the country and whether Lielvārde is ready to receive and support allied air forces.
The Turkish F-16s were one of three allied contributions Melnis requested to protect Latvian airspace during the Oct. 3 election for the 15th Saeima, Latvia’s parliament. Germany sent four Eurofighter jets to Lielvārde for the vote, and Italy also contributed aircraft. Turkish F-16s had briefly visited the base in late August as well.
The deployments follow a series of drone incursions into Baltic airspace that Latvian officials link to Russia’s war against Ukraine. In June, French Rafale jets flying from Lithuania shot down a drone over eastern Latvia, the first time NATO jets downed a stray drone over the country. In August, an Italian Eurofighter shot down another drone that Latvia’s Defense Ministry said had entered Latvian airspace as a result of Russian electronic warfare.

Spain and Greece Refuse to Give Ukraine Patriot Missiles Even as Their Shelf Life Runs Out
Spain and Greece have declined to transfer additional Patriot air defense missiles to Ukraine, despite holding stocks of interceptors approaching the end of their recommended service lives, as Kyiv seeks to strengthen its defenses against Russian missile attacks ahead of winter.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Telegraph on October 9, NATO and European Union officials have been urging both countries to release older Patriot interceptors that could still be used by Ukrainian forces. Greece reportedly holds more than 200 PAC-2 missiles, while the size of Spain’s remaining stockpile is unclear.
The Greek missiles have reportedly been in service for approximately 23 years, approaching the end of their manufacturer-guaranteed operational lifespan. However, reaching that limit does not automatically make the interceptors unusable.
The PAC-2 is designed to engage aircraft and incoming missiles, making it a potential addition to Ukraine’s air defense capabilities as Russia continues targeting Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas raised the issue in September during a visit to Ireland, calling on European countries to make aging interceptors available to Ukraine rather than retain them until their service lives expire.
Spain has already provided limited assistance, announcing the transfer of five Patriot missiles last month. However, Madrid has not agreed to release larger quantities, while Athens has resisted requests to supply its existing stockpile, The Telegraph reported.
The debate comes as Ukraine prepares for another winter of Russian aerial attacks. Ukrainian officials have warned that the country needs at least 300 Patriot interceptors to maintain its defenses against incoming ballistic missiles.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously said Ukraine was securing additional missiles in extremely small quantities, sometimes receiving only one or two interceptors from individual partners. He emphasized that the United States remains the only country capable of supplying the weapons on a substantially larger scale.

articles.title: Yemen hits Riyadh airport again as Saudi flights collapse
articles.body:
Yemen hits Riyadh airport again as Saudi flights collapse
TEHRAN — Riyadh’s airport was hit again on Saturday, two days after Yemeni missiles killed three Saudis there. Regional officials told the Associated Press that air traffic stopped and the airport was evacuated.
A hospital source told Euronews that dozens were injured, at least five in intensive care. Riyadh confirmed the strike by evening but Sanaa had yet to claim it. Three Western embassies warned citizens away, and Kuwait Airways scrapped its Riyadh flights.
Thursday set the pattern. Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority admitted two attacks on King Khalid International Airport, one on facilities and one on a Saudia aircraft, that killed Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami and two other Saudis. CNN verified images of smoke over Terminal 4.
Brigadier General Yahya Saree said Yemeni forces also fired on Najran airport and a Saudi air base. Earlier strikes on Abha and Riyadh airports had already killed three and wounded 36, by Riyadh’s own count.
The commercial damage came fast. Cirium counted 169 of 378 scheduled Riyadh departures cancelled or not operating by late Thursday afternoon, nearly 45 percent.
Lufthansa grounded its Riyadh service through October 16. Turkish Airlines dropped all four departures. Air India, IndiGo and Philippine Airlines followed, and European regulators extended their warnings to Riyadh, Tabuk, Medina and Yanbu.
Saree told airlines, for the last time, that Saudi airspace outside the holy cities is a theater of operations.
Sanaa describes all this as reciprocity. Saudi jets bombed Sanaa International Airport on July 13, after Riyadh threatened Yemen over a flight to Tehran. Human Rights Watch found three munitions on the only working runway, the first coalition strikes since the 2022 truce.
Sanaa declared a blockade of Saudi ports a week later. On Saturday Al Masirah reported four more raids on it. Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, called it an “airport-for-airport equation.”
Riyadh’s answer is “Dawn of Yemen,” the offensive its Yemeni clients launched last Sunday with a stated aim of retaking every area Ansarallah holds, Sanaa included. Its government claims 2,750 strikes in a day and 1,400 fighters “neutralized,” and the coalition says it hit 136 targets.
The same camp claimed Mocha on Tuesday, and Ansarallah answered with video of its fighters inside the city. Saree says Saudi F-15s and Typhoons flew 129 raids in 48 hours in mid-September.
The International Organization for Migration counts more than 200,000 people displaced since September, and UN envoy Hans Grundberg now speaks of full-scale war.
The geography explains Riyadh’s panic. With ongoing developments in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war on Iran, Saudi crude leaves through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu and then past Bab al-Mandab.
Drones hit that pipeline on September 10 and, according to Kpler, flows stopped for at least 11 days. Riyadh blamed launches from Iraq. Ansarallah seized Mayyun Island, also called Perim, in the strait last month.
On Thursday, ten years after the Saudi bombing of Sanaa’s Great Hall killed more than 140 mourners and wounded hundreds, Ansarallah leader Sayyed Abdul-Malik al-Houthi called the war a strategic failure for Riyadh.
He said Yemeni forces can strike enemy assets across the Red Sea and Arabian Sea from anywhere in the country, and accused Riyadh of serving American and Zionist ambitions while posing as guardian of the holy sites.
The kingdom is buying muscle elsewhere. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey activated the so-called Mecca pact on October 5. Pakistan reportedly keeps about 8,000 troops in the kingdom, with JF-17 jets and HQ-9 air defenses, and Reuters reported four planeloads of Pakistani weapons landing in Aden.
Islamabad says its forces will not cross the border. Sanaa’s acting foreign minister, Abdulwahid Abu Ras, has urged Islamabad and Ankara to stay out.
Washington hedges as of now. President Trump reportedly refused the crown prince’s September request for strikes after Ansarallah promised to spare American shipping, though Secretary of State Marco Rubio now vows to honor the U.S. defense commitment.

articles.title: ‘This is not how partners behave’: Zelensky furious over Trump's Russia deal
articles.body:
Russia announced Saturday that it was beginning to lift domestic restrictions on diesel exports following U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement Friday of an agreement to purchase Russian diesel, marking a significant policy reversal after years of American pressure on Moscow over its war in Ukraine.
Axios reported overnight, citing a U.S. official familiar with the matter, that Trump decided to pursue the agreement with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored repeated American requests for Kyiv to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv appeared unwilling to comply with Trump's demands even after the agreement. Ukraine launched an overnight attack on Russia involving some 500 drones, according to the report, including a strike on an oil facility in the Rostov region.
The American official criticized Zelensky, saying he was misreading the situation and that continued Ukrainian attacks on refineries were undermining the trust the Ukrainian president had built with Trump over the past six months.
Zelensky sharply criticized the U.S.-Russia agreement Friday, accusing Washington of exploiting negotiations with the Ukrainian delegation as cover for its own dealings with Moscow.
"I believe our team is simply being used as cover. This is certainly not fair and not how partners should treat each other," Zelensky said.
Ukrainian media reports noted that officials in Kyiv doubted the agreement would achieve Trump's objective of lowering global fuel prices. They nevertheless acknowledged that the deal itself weakened Ukraine's negotiating position.
Russian petroleum exports have been restricted by both international sanctions and domestic export bans imposed after Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities disrupted production and caused fuel shortages inside Russia.
Now, according to Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, who oversees the country's energy sector, Moscow is beginning to lift those restrictions ahead of schedule.
Trump announced on his Truth Social platform that he had reached the agreement during a phone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. The two leaders had been expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia.
Instead, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and an additional 1 million tons shortly afterward. Russia would then supply another 3 million tons within a relatively short period, he added.
Warm exchanges between Trump and Putin
Senior Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the conversation to Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency.
"The conversation lasted an hour and a half, and neither side wanted to be the first to hang up," Ushakov said. He added that Trump had expressed his willingness to continue speaking with Putin that evening, overnight and the following day.
Putin's economic adviser Kirill Dmitriev, meanwhile, posted several messages on social media thanking Trump for the agreement. One of the posts consisted of a single word: "Diesel."
Ushakov and Kremlin-aligned media sought to portray the agreement as evidence of a new phase in relations between Moscow and Washington, arguing that it demonstrated Russia could no longer be considered internationally isolated.
Describing the personal exchanges between the two presidents, Ushakov said Trump had warmly congratulated Putin on his 74th birthday earlier in the week. Trump wished Putin success and conveyed greetings from first lady Melania Trump, Ushakov said.
"Vladimir Putin thanked his American counterpart for the congratulations and warm words," the senior Russian official said, adding that Moscow appreciated the attention Trump and his team were devoting to dialogue with Russia despite domestic U.S. issues and developments in the Middle East.
On the ground, however, Russian attacks deep inside Ukraine continued to exact a heavy toll on civilians.
Overnight, Moscow launched a missile attack on the southern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia. According to Ukrainian media reports, at least seven people were killed when a residential building suffered a direct hit. Local authorities said another 14 people were missing.

articles.title: Iran slams Macron’s double standard on nuclear deterrence
articles.body:
In a post on X on Friday, Esmaeil Baghaei said that during a test of a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, Emmanuel Macron said that in order to be free, one must be feared, and to be feared, one must be powerful.

He added that they intend to remain powerful themselves, armed with nuclear weapons and, of course, formidable, while imposing restrictions on others, including countries that merely seek to use nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, by raising the specter of a supposed “nuclear threat.”
“A peace in which nuclear powers regard their own weapons as guarantors of their freedom and security, but label the same logic a threat when invoked by others, is not true peace. It is a monopoly of power based on a sense of superiority.”

articles.title: Putin Rejects Peace Talks in Trump Call, Vows to Press War
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin rejected the resumption of peace negotiations and reaffirmed Moscow’s intention to continue the war against Ukraine until all Kremlin objectives are fulfilled during a telephone conversation with US President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told Russian state media.
According to Ushakov, Putin made it clear during the exchange that Russia will sustain combat operations without diplomatic concessions.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Putin made it clear that Moscow will continue hostilities until it achieves all stated goals,” Ushakov said.
The Kremlin aide claimed that Trump initiated the call to extend warm birthday greetings to the Russian leader, wishing him success and passing along regards from First Lady Melania Trump.
In response, however, Putin reiterated Russia’s unyielding terms regarding Ukraine, dismissing prospects for an early negotiated settlement.
Ushakov added that Putin accused Ukraine of attempting to disrupt elections in Russia and asserted that Ukrainian resistance is futile, claiming Russian forces hold the operational initiative across the front lines.
Ushakov further claimed that following the discussion, Trump instructed American officials to relay the diplomatic “signals” received from the Kremlin directly to the Ukrainian government.
Hardline stance despite diplomatic overtures
Putin’s refusal to consider peace talks comes despite intensive diplomatic maneuvering by Washington to initiate a negotiating framework ahead of winter.
Easing Diesel Sanctions Shows Weakness to Putin, Sybiha Says
On Friday, Oct. 9, high-level multilateral consultations convened by the US in Miami – bringing together US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators, and representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO – concluded after a six-hour session without a announced breakthrough.
While Witkoff characterized the dialogue as constructive, European and Ukrainian officials expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to engage in substantive de-escalation.
Putin’s uncompromising posture in the phone call also aligns with public warnings issued by Ukrainian leaders.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Friday that concessions to Moscow project Western weakness, asserting that Putin interprets economic and diplomatic overtures as appeasement rather than incentives for peace.
The Trump diesel pact
The phone call and Putin’s subsequent rebuff unfolded alongside controversy surrounding Trump’s announcement of a bilateral commercial agreement permitting Russian petroleum shipments into American and global markets.
Trump announced that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel immediately, with 500,000 tons scheduled for November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling up to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Trump argued that the deliveries, combined with what he termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” would curb fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid energy market volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Shortly after the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sanctions waiver was enacted just three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which was designed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky had directly appealed to visiting US lawmakers to strictly enforce statutory sanctions as a vital tool to compel Moscow to negotiate.
The sanctions relief granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since July, when Russia imposed an export ban on domestic diesel following successful Ukrainian drone strikes that damaged major Russian refining facilities.
Trump had previously urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, attributing elevated diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction operations rather than the Middle Eastern conflict.

articles.title: Trump's diesel agreement with Putin accused of contradicting Russia sanctions law
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's Friday announcement that Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war by targeting Russian energy exports.
Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.
But commentators and critics were quick to highlight contradictions between the new policy and prior efforts by the U.S. to clamp down on Russian oil sales.
Those efforts most recently included the enactment of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, empowering Trump to impose tariffs up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, among other restrictions. Trump signed the bill into law just three weeks ago.
"Congress just passed a law giving Trump the power to impose new tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil & gas," Scott Lincicome, vice president of the libertarian Cato Institute, said on X after Trump's Friday announcement.
"Can America tariff America?" he quipped.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, accused Trump's latest move of being "directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill."
Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown University Law Center's Institute of International Economic Law, in an X post said that the relaxation of Russian diesel restrictions "pretty much proves the point that the Graham Russia Bill was not going to force the Trump Administration to increase economic pressure on Moscow."
Some of the criticism crossed party lines.
"Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin's war to an end with a negotiated settlement," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said in an X post. "Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," McCaul said.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's questions about the diesel agreement with Russia.
Less than a year earlier, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on multiple Russian oil companies in response to what it called "Russia's lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine."
Trump also had previously slammed NATO allies for continuing to buy Russian oil. In a September 2025 Truth Social post, he wrote, "the purchase of Russian Oil, by some, has been shocking! It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia."
Later that month, Trump again harangued world leaders for doing business with Russia.
"They're funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that one?" he said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. "They can't be doing what they're doing. They're buying oil and gas from Russia while they're fighting Russia."
Trump announced the diesel deal in a Truth Social post Friday afternoon after what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the agreement, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then another 500,000 tons in November, followed by 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" and 3 million more depending on refinery conditions, Trump wrote.
The Treasury Department soon after said that Trump directed the Office of Foreign Assets Control to immediately issue a "temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market." OFAC specified that the sanctioned transactions will be authorized for about six months, until April 7.
Russia seemed to celebrate the move. "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world," an X account associated with Putin's economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev said in response to the announcement.
But Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose military has started targeting Russian oil refineries, said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
"We count on America's fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia," he said.
"A strong one, not a weak one," he added.
Trump thanked Putin later Friday afternoon for enabling "massive amounts of oil" to come to the U.S.
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it," Trump told reporters before heading to Syracuse, New York.
The Trump administration has previously eased some Russian energy sanctions temporarily, though more narrowly than Friday's announcement.
Earlier this year, in an attempt to stabilize markets after the start of the Iran war, the Trump administration issued limited, 30-day waivers allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil that was already in transit.
But some interpreted the latest move as a more significant step.
"It looks like Trump cut a deal with the devil," Jeremy Siegel, professor emeritus of finance at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" Friday afternoon.
"It's not a permanent solution at all. It's sort of a short-term Band Aid," Siegel said. "And cutting back on or eliminating sanctions on Russia for the invasion in Ukraine, I think, is a very unfortunate consequence."

articles.title: Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
articles.body:
Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
US President Donald Trump’s top envoys have begun two days of negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives in Miami, focusing on preparations for the coming winter and potential ways to de-escalate the Ukraine conflict on terms that would be acceptable to Moscow.
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Friday’s discussions as “constructive,” saying American representatives had discussed prospects for a “lasting peace” with Kiev and its most hawkish European backers, including Britain, France and Germany, as well as officials from the European Commission and NATO.
The talks covered “near-term measures related to winter preparedness,” including energy resilience and grain exports, as well as longer-term security guarantees, post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s potential accession to the EU, according to Witkoff.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on X.
Today, representatives from the United States, the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO met in Miami and held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace. The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession. The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia. Participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to continuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable peace that strengthens security and creates opportunities for lasting stability and prosperity.
— Special Envoy Steve Witkoff (@SEPeaceMissions) October 9, 2026
The negotiations were scheduled to continue on Saturday, and no concrete agreements or breakthroughs have been announced so far.
The US delegation is led by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Kiev is represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, deputy chief of staff Sergey Kislitsa and senior lawmaker David Arakhamia.
The European delegation reportedly includes Bjoern Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany. NATO is represented by Geoffrey van Leeuwen, chief of staff to Secretary General Mark Rutte, according to European media reports.
The talks follow reports that Witkoff and Kushner were preparing to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the diplomatic deadlock. According to Axios, the pair could travel to Moscow later this month for further talks with Putin.
One proposal under consideration reportedly involves a partial ceasefire covering strikes on energy infrastructure, amid growing anxiety among Kiev’s European backers over the economic and energy consequences of the conflict.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source previously told AFP.
The Miami meeting also coincided with a 90-minute phone conversation between Trump and Putin on Friday, during which the leaders discussed Ukraine, Iran and a major agreement to resume Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets.
Zelensky lashed out at Trump, effectively accusing Washington of stabbing Kiev in the back by striking a separate diesel deal with Moscow. Zelensky branded the move “a weak decision by strong partners” and accused the US of using talks with the Ukrainian delegation in Miami as a “smokescreen” while negotiating with Putin behind Kiev’s back.
Trump has repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for American consumers. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Trump promised Putin that he would convey Moscow’s position to the Ukrainian delegation in Florida.

articles.title: ‘We’re being used as a front,’ Zelensky says of Trump’s diesel deal with Putin
articles.body:
Russia and the U.S. have agreed on a deal to supply Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets. President Donald Trump announced the agreement on the evening of October 9 after a phone call with Vladimir Putin. Trump called the talks “highly successful.” Putin confirmed that Russia is ready to supply oil and petroleum products to the U.S. and global markets.
The U.S. said it is easing sanctions on Russian diesel. The Treasury Department has already issued a temporary license allowing sales of Russian diesel on the global market through April 7, 2027, despite U.S. sanctions. Washington previously eased sanctions on Russian oil temporarily because of a market crisis caused by the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran.
Russia has also begun lifting restrictions on diesel exports, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said. Sanctions and domestic export bans restrict exports of Russian oil and petroleum products worldwide. A ban on diesel and marine fuel exports by producers, for example, remains in effect through the end of October. Russia imposed it amid Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and a domestic fuel crisis caused by Ukrainian attacks over the summer.
Trump said the two sides agreed on the “immediate” delivery of more than 300,000 metric tons of Russian diesel. Russia will supply another 500,000 metric tons in November, followed by an additional million metric tons. Novak said Russia is ready to supply additional diesel to the U.S. market as early as October. Exports are also expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after repairs.
Ukraine criticized the diesel deal between Moscow and Washington. President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media that any easing of sanctions on Russia without agreements on de-escalation shows “obvious weakness.” “Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” he said.
The deal comes as talks on ending the war resume. A Ukrainian delegation is reportedly meeting with U.S. negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Miami on October 9 and 10. Reuters reported that the national security advisers of the U.K., France, and Germany, along with representatives of NATO and the EU, were invited to the talks. Axios reported that the U.S. negotiators plan to present the Ukrainian delegation with “new ideas and proposals” and then discuss them with Russia. No details of the proposals were given. “I think our team is simply being used as a front. That’s certainly dishonest, and it’s certainly no way to treat a partner,” Zelensky told reporters after the U.S. announced the diesel deal.
Russian authorities asked the U.S. to lift sanctions as part of talks on an “energy truce,” sources told The Kyiv Independent on the eve of the diesel deal. Officials in Kyiv said Ukraine was ready to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Russia agreed to stop striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Trump, who is under pressure over rising U.S. fuel prices ahead of the congressional midterm elections, has repeatedly demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian oil facilities. He said the attacks were causing global fuel shortages and price increases.
Putin rejected the idea of an “energy truce” with Kyiv on October 2. Speaking at the Valdai forum, he said stopping the strikes alone would not solve the problem of high diesel prices in the U.S. and around the world unless sanctions on Russia were lifted.

articles.title: Trump Makes Deal With Putin On Diesel Exports. Ukraine Calls It A 'Gift'
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- US President Donald Trump said he reached an agreement with President Vladimir Putin to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a move Ukraine immediately criticized as a "gift" to the Kremlin.
Seeking to contain soaring energy prices, Trump said in a social media post on October 9 that the two leaders agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another million after that.
The move will see prices "COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote.
Diesel futures fell about 4 percent after the announcement but remained more than 110 percent higher than at the start of the year. Brent crude traded at around $104 a barrel, down just 0.3 percent on the day.
The decision came as Ukrainian, US, and European officials held talks in Miami aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine. The discussions concluded without a breakthrough.
The waiver drew critical comments from Kyiv to lawmakers in Washington, who warned that easing restrictions could provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war against Ukraine.
It also raised questions about US policy toward Russia following Trump’s recent signing of legislation intended to tighten sanctions against countries supporting Moscow’s energy trade.
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in a post on social media.
"Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."
To enable the flow of diesel, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale, delivery, and import of Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said that after the initial flows, Russia would supply a further 3 million tons “within a short period of time.”
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was ready to increase supplies in October, with exports expected to rise in November and December as refineries resume operations after maintenance.
Diesel prices have climbed since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran in February, sparking a conflict that is now in its eighth month.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing prices higher and urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian energy facilities.
“The problem I have with Ukraine and Russia is that, you know, a lot of the diesel comes … from Russia, and the Russia plants are being hit by Ukraine,” Trump told reporters recently.
Ukrainian officials have said they are prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if Moscow halted its recent barrage of strikes on Ukraine’s energy and other civilian infrastructure installations.
As Ukraine’s negotiating team was in Florida, Zelenskyy also questioned the purpose of the Miami talks while Washington was allowing Russia to earn money from fuel exports.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” he said.
Earlier on October 9, Zelenskyy welcomed a bipartisan delegation of US senators to Kyiv and called for stronger pressure on Moscow.
Meanwhile, on Capitol Hill, the waiver for Russia drew the ire of several lawmakers.
“It surely looks bad. The president has always had a moral blindness when it comes to Putin. Propping up Russia’s war economy is terrible,” Republican Representative Don Bacon told RFE/RL.
Democrat Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the bipartisan Russia sanctions legislation, called the decision an embarrassment, arguing that it would benefit Russia and China while undermining congressional efforts to pressure Moscow.
“This poorly concealed attempt to mitigate the havoc caused by Trump’s illegal war in Iran will only benefit the Chinese & Russian economies & lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine,” he wrote on social media.
Blumenthal called the agreement “a stain on our nation’s character” and said it ran counter to Congress’s intent in its recent passing of a sanctions bill.
He also warned US companies considering purchases of Russian fuel: “Congress is watching.”
Daniel Fried, a former US diplomat and sanctions expert, also criticized the timing of the waiver.
“General License allowing sale of Russian diesel, proceeds of which support Russia’s war against Ukraine. Not a promising start to the imminent talks on ending the war,” Fried said in a social media post.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the move showed Trump was prioritizing the Iran conflict and its economic consequences over pressure on Russia.
“The Russia legislation put the onus, and the ability to act, in President Trump's hands,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
“Today's diesel license shows Trump is prioritizing the Iran conflict over pressure on Russia, and he likely doesn't intend to use a lot of the authorities in the bill,” she said.
Ukrainian sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said the waiver could also undermine Trump’s argument that Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries were the main driver of rising diesel prices.
“If limiting diesel sanctions on Russia provides market relief then it’s clear the primary impact to the global diesel market was the Iran conflict and blockade, not Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, which would have had a secondary impact,” Vlasiuk told RFE/RL. “It lines up with price timelines.”
The decision also raises questions about the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022, which prohibits Russian oil imports into the United States unless the president certifies that Russia has agreed to withdraw from Ukraine, recognized Ukrainian sovereignty, and poses no threat to NATO.
Supplied materials from officials on the decision does not establish how that provision applies to the new license.
The Miami discussions, initially expected to last two days, concluded on Friday, October 9, according to US envoy Steve Witkoff.
Representatives from the United States, the E3 group of European countries, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO held “constructive discussions” on ways to de-escalate and end the war before winter.
Witkoff said the agenda included winter preparedness, energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees, longer-term security arrangements for Ukraine and Europe, and support for Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction and eventual European Union accession.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on social media.
The Kremlin said Trump and Putin had also discussed prospects for resolving the war during their phone call, alongside the situation surrounding Iran and other bilateral issues.

articles.title: Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
articles.body:
Trump lifted Russian fuel ban after Zelensky rejected his demands – Axios
US President Donald Trump’s decision to approve a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel exports came after Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, Axios reported on Saturday, citing a US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
Trump has persistently blamed Ukraine, and Zelensky personally, for exacerbating the global fuel crisis, accusing authorities in Kiev of deliberately targeting Russian refining facilities and driving up prices for American consumers. Despite repeated warnings from Washington, the Ukrainian leader pledged earlier this month to ramp up the long-range strikes.
“The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too,” the US official told the news outlet.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators during eight hours of talks in Miami earlier this week that Trump planned to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened to cut off US intelligence sharing with Kiev if it continued to ignore Trump’s requests to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, but the US official denied that any such threat had been made.
The media outlet cited the official as saying that the dispute over the diesel deal emerged as the US mediators conducted constructive talks on ending the conflict with Ukrainian and European diplomats. The negotiations reportedly focused on finalizing security guarantees for Ukraine from the US, Europe, and NATO, as well as new territorial proposals.
The official added that Witkoff and Kushner had presented postwar plans covering Ukraine’s reconstruction, military funding, and budget deficits, while participants discussed Kiev’s potential EU accession, its future relationship with NATO, and a possible postwar security framework between Europe and Russia.
Trump and Putin held a phone call on Friday, shortly after which the US Treasury Department announced a temporary waiver of sanctions on Russian fuel trade, allowing diesel to be sold, delivered, and exported, including into the US, until at least April 7, 2027.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and a million tons thereafter, with up to three million additional tons available “within a short period of time.”
The Kremlin said Moscow was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to global markets, adding that this would benefit the world economy. Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak also confirmed that Russia would lift diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule, with the process to begin “immediately.”
Russia had previously extended restrictions on diesel, ship fuel, and gas oil exports until October 31 to stabilize the domestic market amid seasonal demand from the harvest. Fuel producers are barred from exporting until October 31, while fuel resellers face a ban until January 31, 2027. Gasoline exports are also prohibited until the end of January.

articles.body:
Ukraine intends to press ahead with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries despite a bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and international markets, the Financial Times reported.
A senior Ukrainian official dismissed US calls to halt operations against Moscow’s energy infrastructure, signaling that Kyiv will not adjust its asymmetric targeting strategy.

“We will burn [Russian] refineries,” the senior official told the Financial Times.
The vow comes as energy market analysts question Moscow’s physical ability to fulfill the commercial commitments announced by the White House, citing extensive degradation across the Russian petrochemical sector caused by repeated Ukrainian interdiction operations.
According to data cited by the Financial Times, Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of their installed capacity due to operational halts, emergency repairs, and equipment deficits resulting from Ukrainian strikes.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at energy intelligence firm Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Russian refining deficit
Industry data highlights the extent of the contraction across Russia’s downstream petroleum sector over the past year.
Russia Exploits School Knife Attacks for Disinformation
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel fuel per month by sea, according to Kpler records.
However, maritime shipments fell precipitously throughout 2026 as successive Ukrainian drone waves damaged primary distillation units, cracking facilities, and storage hubs across European Russia and western Siberia.
With domestic refining capacity constrained, the Kremlin enacted strict restrictions on petroleum product outflows in July, effectively prohibiting domestic diesel exports to prevent localized fuel deficits and inflation within the Russian domestic market.
Outside rare exceptional consignments, seaborne diesel exports have effectively ceased.
The Financial Times also noted that the US has historically accounted for a negligible share of Russian refined petroleum consumption.
Washington has not imported Russian diesel fuel since July 2022, following early sanctions enacted in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During periods when American importers did purchase Russian diesel, volumes averaged approximately 77,000 metric tons per month, peaking at 210,000 metric tons in January 2022.
The Trump diesel pact
The dispute over refining strikes follows Trump’s announcement on Truth Social that Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.
Trump indicated that deliveries could scale up to 3 million tons within a short timeframe, though he acknowledged that shipments would depend on the condition of Russian refineries.
The US president claimed that the bilateral deal, alongside US naval operations in the Strait of Hormuz, would quickly alleviate fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The regulatory exemption was granted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which aimed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The sanctions waiver granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since its July export ban, when Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov asserted that Russian fuel could ease international benchmarks only if granted unrestricted market access.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukrainian officials to suspend strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, attributing high diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction rather than shipping disruptions in the Middle East.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone destroys Pantsir on Russian ‘Flakturm’
articles.body:
- The SBU’s Alpha unit released footage of a drone destroying a Russian Pantsir air defense system mounted on a “Flakturm”-style air defense tower.
- The SBU did not disclose the location, date or drone type used in the strike.
A Ukrainian drone has destroyed a Russian Pantsir air defense system on top of a “Flakturm,” one of the purpose-built anti-aircraft towers Russia has been putting up to stop Ukrainian drones, according to new footage released by the Security Service of Ukraine’s Alpha special operations unit.
The video shows the strike on the elevated platform, which Russia built to raise the air defense system above trees and terrain. The Security Service of Ukraine, known as the SBU, did not say where or when the strike took place, what type of drone was used, or whether the tower itself was destroyed along with the Pantsir.
The towers are widely nicknamed Flakturms after the Flaktürme, the massive concrete anti-aircraft towers Nazi Germany built to defend Berlin, Hamburg and Vienna from Allied bombers during World War II. Russia’s use of them became public in September 2023, when state television channel Russia-24 broadcast footage of Pantsir systems mounted on metal towers around Moscow.
Russia places air defense systems on these raised platforms to give their radars a clearer view of low-flying drones and to extend the distance at which they can spot targets. Ground-based radars have trouble seeing small drones that fly close to the ground or behind obstacles, and lifting the system several meters higher helps the radar look over them. The tradeoff is that a tower cannot move. Once its position is known, Ukrainian drone units can plan precision strikes against a target that will still be there when the drone arrives.
The Pantsir is a truck-mounted short-range air defense system that combines a radar, surface-to-air missiles and twin 30 mm cannons. It is one of the main systems Russia uses to shoot down drones and cruise missiles, and Ukrainian forces have made it a priority target. SBU head Vasyl Malyuk said in late 2025 that Ukraine had destroyed 48% of Russia’s Pantsir systems since the start of that year, adding that Russia builds about 30 a year, fewer than Ukraine was destroying.
The strike adds to a series of Ukrainian attacks on Russian air defenses this month. Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces hit another Pantsir-S1 near Kudepsta in Russia’s Krasnodar region on Oct. 8 and into Oct. 9, and Ukrainian FP-2 strike drones destroyed a Pantsir-S2 earlier in October, according to footage published online.

articles.title: Zelensky Warns Against Easing Russia Sanctions as US Authorizes Russian Diesel Sales Through 2027
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump announced in a post on Truth Social Media that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets. Another 500,000 tons would follow in November and 1 million tons after that.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” Trump wrote, adding that Russia would then deliver 3 million tons of diesel within a short time, depending on the condition of its diesel refineries.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Combined with what he called a “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” the deal would quickly bring down diesel prices for Americans and the rest of the world, Trump claimed.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The new license came only three weeks after Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, appearing to completely disregard the bill intended to target Russia’s energy and defense industries, as well as networks close to Putin.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky appealed to the visiting US lawmakers to enforce the law, as it remains crucial for ending the war.
The move also gives Moscow something it had openly demanded. In late September, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russian diesel could flood international markets – but only if it reached them without sanctions or restrictions.
Sybiha Presses WTO Chief on Black Sea Shipping, Remote Audits
Since July, Russia has banned nearly all of its diesel exports, after Ukrainian drone strikes managed to halt a large share of its refining capacity.
Meanwhile, Trump has repeatedly pressed Kyiv to ease those strikes, pinning the blame on Ukraine for record diesel prices instead of the US-Iran war.
Zelensky warns against sanctions relief
Zelensky argued that easing sanctions on Russia without a clear and durable de-escalation agreement would be a sign of weakness that benefits Moscow. “In my view, this is a weak decision,” he said.
The Ukrainian president appeared to respond directly to Trump’s announcement. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he said.
Zelensky also pointed to the EU’s decision to delist two Russian oligarchs – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman – both closely connected to Putin and the Kremlin’s war effort.
Since that move, he said, Russian strikes and terror of civilians have only intensified.
When the US lawmakers asked what it would take to end the war, Zelensky listed three conditions:
- enforcement of sanctions under the law championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham
- support for Ukraine in protecting lives
- and sustained pressure on Russia over the war.
De-escalation offered – again
Zelensky reiterated that Kyiv is prepared to take de-escalation steps that match Russia’s own, and that the American negotiating team is aware of this position.
Zelensky framed Ukraine’s long-range strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities as a response to Moscow’s years-long campaign against Ukraine’s power grid. Halting them, he said, would depend on Russia ending its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Moscow, however, has repeatedly rejected such arrangements. In the very few times it had agreed to a ceasefire, it failed to honor it, with attacks resuming immediately.
The president stressed that any easing of the conflict must be reciprocal rather than one-sided, and pointed to Russia’s results on the battlefield. In his view, Russia is relying on strikes against civilians to make up for its failure to reach its military goals.
This year, he said, Russian forces are weaker on the front line than at any earlier point in the war.
“That is exactly why Putin relies on terror. That is exactly why he relies on attempts at backroom deals on one or another easing of pressure on Russia, to buy more time and more opportunities for war.”

articles.title: US, Ukrainians, Europeans discuss 'new ideas' to end war
articles.body:
US, Europe and Ukraine hold 'constructive discussions' on joint plan to end war
US, Ukrainian and European negotiators held talks in Miami on Friday to seek a common proposal to end the war in Ukraine, as President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel drew criticism from lawmakers and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
US, Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Friday in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with Washington seeking a way out of the dangerous stalemate.
The talks were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to boost diesel supplies, underscoring how the conflict has become entwined with soaring energy prices.
Read moreTrump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the "constructive discussions" tackled "potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace".
Witkoff said the meeting included "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO".
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and "longer-term arrangements for Ukraine's and Europe's security to prevent future conflict", Witkoff said.
He also noted the "productive" exchange discussed supporting Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession.
Witkoff did not say if the parties would meet on Saturday as originally planned.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Thursday that the conflict had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
"The other way that stalemates end is through escalation," Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighboring NATO countries.
"We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict," he added.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.
Following a telephone call with Putin on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November.

The US Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license to allow Russian diesel to flow to global markets. It was not immediately clear whether Trump and Putin had discussed Ukraine during their call.
New proposals
The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Kushner, the president's son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.
US negotiators have since been developing fresh proposals with Russian and Ukrainian officials, a source familiar with the discussions told AFP.
With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement.
The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk that killed 30 people.
Territorial deadlock
Trump's repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow's sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.
Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.
European officials have expressed concern over high energy costs and the wider economic consequences of the conflict, according to the US sources.
Witkoff and Kushner briefed the president on their latest proposals on Thursday at a meeting also attended by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior officials, Axios reported.
The US administration hopes to make diplomatic headway before November's midterm elections, with Washington also seeking to arrange broader talks involving Russia and Ukraine later this month.
The Kremlin has signaled that such three-way negotiations could resume in October, although no date has been announced.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.

Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".
"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.
He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
- Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices 
  - Published20 hours ago
- Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people 
  - Published4 hours ago
Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".
He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".
"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."
The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.
"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.
Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
- Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? 
  - Published23 hours ago
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.
But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.
Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.
Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

articles.title: Ukraine’s ADF down 117 out of 160 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine’s ADF down 117 out of 160 drones used by Russia to attack Ukraine overnight
As reported by Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine said this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on October 9, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 160 strike UAVs, including Shahed-type drones (110 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the areas of Oryol, Kursk, Shatalovo, Millerovo and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air assault was repelled by Ukrainian fighter aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 9:00 on Saturday, October 10, air defense forces had shot down or suppressed 117 drones.
Hits were recorded at 14 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
